The FI community has a saying: financial independence is not about quitting your job — it is about having the freedom to choose whether to keep it. Every dollar you save and invest is a vote for your future autonomy. When you have 12-24 months of expenses saved, you negotiate from strength. When you reach Coast FI or beyond, a bad job becomes a choice, not a trap. Build your FI runway and the question changes from "Can I afford to quit?" to "Does this role still serve my goals?".

Work through these steps before making your decision.

It has been revealed that have you consistently wanted to leave for 30+ days? If no, wait. Temporary frustration is not a reason to upend your career. If yes, proceed to step two.

According to recent reports, pro tip: Keep a brief daily journal noting your satisfaction level 1-10. Data beats feelings for decision-making.

Is the problem your boss, your role, your compensation, the culture, or the industry? Some problems follow you to the next job. A bad manager is fixable by transferring. An industry you hate requires a bigger change.

It has been revealed that verify your emergency fund, health insurance options, debt situation, and FI runway. If you are not financially ready, keep working while you build your safety net and search for alternatives.

Before quitting, have you requested a transfer, a raise, a role change, or a conversation with HR? Many solvable problems go unaddressed because employees assume the answer will be no.

Pro tip: A direct conversation with your manager about your concerns resolves the issue 40% of the time.

If you decide to leave, secure your next opportunity (if possible), give appropriate notice, document your work for your successor, and maintain every professional relationship.

It has been revealed that pro tip: Never burn bridges. The colleague you leave today may be the hiring manager at your dream company in three years.

At minimum, 3-6 months of essential expenses in a liquid savings account. If you are quitting without another job lined up, aim for 6-12 months. The FI community recommends having your emergency fund fully funded, health insurance secured, and ideally some progress toward financial independence to provide a psychological safety net.

If your job is causing persistent anxiety, depression, or physical health symptoms that do not improve with coping strategies, therapy, or workplace changes — yes, your health must come first. But do it strategically: secure health insurance, build your financial runway, and consult a therapist or career coach before making the leap. Never make a permanent career decision during a temporary emotional crisis.

In a recent development, generally, quitting gives you more control over the narrative, timing, and terms. Being fired can qualify you for unemployment benefits (quitting usually does not), but it can also create a negative reference. If you sense a termination is coming, consider whether negotiating a mutual separation with severance is an option. Document everything and consult an employment attorney if you believe the termination may be discriminatory or retaliatory.

Be honest and frame it positively. Acceptable explanations include: career transition (took time to retrain or earn a certification), personal development (traveled, volunteered, or cared for family), or strategic job search (took time to find the right fit rather than settling). Employers increasingly accept career gaps — especially post-2020 — as long as you can articulate what you did during the time off.

COBRA (Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) lets you continue your employer health plan for up to 18 months after leaving. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer contributed) plus a 2% admin fee. Individual coverage typically costs $500-$700/month and family coverage runs $1,400-$2,000+/month. The ACA marketplace is often cheaper, especially if your income drops after leaving.

Industry observers note that FI savings transform the equation entirely. With a substantial portfolio, you have a financial runway that removes the urgency and desperation from the decision. Even partial FI — having 2-5 years of expenses invested — means you can quit a toxic job, take time to find the right next role, or transition to lower-paying but more fulfilling work. FI is not just about retiring early; it is about having the leverage to make career decisions from a position of strength rather than fear.

The question "should I quit my job?" deserves a framework, not an impulse. Apply the 30-day test, diagnose the real problem, verify your financial readiness, explore internal solutions, and then make a deliberate decision. If you have been building toward financial independence, your savings give you something most people lack: the freedom to walk away from a bad situation without financial panic. FI is the ultimate career insurance — it turns "I have to stay" into "I choose to stay or go." Build your runway, protect your reputation, and make the decision from a position of strength.

A housing development in Andorra designed by French studio Ateliers Jean Nouvel and Spanish studio Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos has been damaged in a fire.

Called La Querola, the project is shortlisted in the housing category of this year’s Dezeen Awards and recently won the awards’ public vote. The cause of the fire is unknown and no official estimate of the extent of the damage has been released so far.

In Shanghai, access to the staircase of the Grand Opera House by international studio Snøhetta has been restricted to ticket holders.

Access to the spiral staircase, which leads up to the roof and has become a popular spot for photos, now costs £5.60 per person. Snøhetta told Dezeen that “visitor management is necessary”.

In car news, Swedish brand Polestar has unveiled its Formula 2030 concept car that the brand indicates “screams performance”.

The low-slung sports car has signature Dual Blade headlights and was intended to project power, with a long bonnet, wraparound windscreen, short overhangs, muscular haunches and 22-inch wheels.

Regional Canon offices worldwide have issued an urgent service notice regarding the firm’s RF1.4x and RF2x extenders, commonly known as teleconverters. Canon warns that if users suspect anything unusual about how their extender feels in use, they should request an inspection and repair through Canon.

Canon Rumors claims this is a known issue with Canon RF-mount extenders, where a lens can feel like it is locked onto the extender even when it isn’t. In some cases, a lens could even detach from the extender and fall to the ground. Given that extenders are commonly used with expensive telephoto lenses, this could be an extremely costly problem.

Canon Malaysia’s notice on the matter is particularly interesting, offering slightly more information than the service notice from Canon U.S.A. and others.

Recent findings suggest that “We regret to inform that a potential matter has been confirmed for Extender RF1.4x/RF2x,” Canon Malaysia says, which goes further than what Canon U.S.A. writes.

Recent findings suggest that canon U.S.A. stops short of mentioning any issue, only issuing a “service notice” and noting that Canon RF extender people should always check the following:.

Canon U.S.A. adds that if photographers notice “anything unusual,” which could include the lens release lever feeling “stiff” or like it is “catching on something and cannot be operated smoothly,” there is a chance the RF lens is not locked in place.

“If used in this state, the RF lens may come off,” Canon continues.

Any affected users, or those who have any concerns about the operation of their RF extenders, should contact the Canon Customer Support Center in their region for an inspection and, if necessary, a free repair.

Sources indicate that in any case, it is not immediately clear what the exact issue is, what causes it, or how it might be fixed. Given that Canon is offering free repairs, though, it is reasonable to speculate that there is a physical component that needs to be fixed to ensure the consistently safe operation of Canon RF extenders.

According to recent reports, any photographers with Canon RF extenders should carefully inspect them before use and, if worried at all, contact their local Canon customer support team. A lens falling off an extender is a significant risk.

PetaPixel has reached out to Canon for comment and will update this story if it hears back.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For audiences who associate the US photographer Nan Goldin with the friends and lovers of her slideshow The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1973-86), her forthcoming Hayward Gallery exhibition may come as a surprise. Animals, a solar eclipse and footage salvaged from nature documentaries will feature in Goldin’s first institutional solo show in the UK since her 2002 retrospective at the Whitechapel Gallery.

According to recent reports, what links these subjects to the photographs that established her reputation? According to the Hayward’s chief curator, Rachel Thomas, the connection lies in the relationships Goldin creates through the camera, rather than the identities of those who appear before it. In Thomas’s reading, Goldin’s focus on queer communities and chosen family has widened to embrace the natural world.

Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part II, 2026.

© Nan Goldin, courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

Rather than being a retrospective, the exhibition You Never Did Anything Wrong presents new and recent work by Goldin. Thomas, who worked with the photographer at the Irish Museum of Modern Art in 2017, tells The Art Newspaper: “I wanted to collaborate again to reveal where her practice is moving now.” Four years in the making, the exhibition is the Hayward’s contribution to the Southbank Centre’s 75th-anniversary programme devoted to “visionaries who have fundamentally redefined culture”.

The show’s centrepiece will be the premiere of You never did anything wrong, Part II (2026). Created with the film-maker David Sherman, it draws on 16mm nature documentaries from the 1960s and 70s, and damaged soundtracks from old films, with a fresh score by the British musician Mica Levi. Goldin turns material associated with explaining the natural world into an abstract meditation on animals, land and impending extinction.

Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part I, 2024.

© Nan Goldin, courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

It has been revealed that it accompanies You never did anything wrong, Part I (2024), which centres on a solar eclipse and draws on a myth of animals stealing the sun. Together, the films bring Goldin’s work into a world without human protagonists.

Industry observers note that elsewhere, Stendhal Syndrome (2024), receiving its UK premiere, places photographs of her friends and lovers in dialogue with classical art, accompanied by a score by Soundwalk Collective. Memory Lost (2019-21), meanwhile, returns to addiction, connecting personal experience to Goldin’s campaigning with Pain (Prescription Addiction Intervention Now), the group she founded to confront the opioid crisis in the US.

Art of intimacy: Young Love (2024) is one of Goldin’s works in Stendhal Syndrome © Nan Goldin; courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

Recent findings suggest that for Thomas, compassion connects these changing subjects. Goldin’s importance lies partly in her refusal to maintain a distance from the people she photographs, with the exhibition proposing that this approach can extend beyond her own community. “What endures across every medium and chapter is an exploration of compassion,” Thomas says. “Goldin simply expands the horizon of who and what is embraced by her gaze.”.

• You Never Did Anything Wrong, Hayward Gallery, London, 24 November-14 March 2027.

Recent findings suggest that “You’re gonna love how it feels,” says the app’s developer, Not Boring. “I guarantee it.”.

Its proprietary SuperRaw mode promises “film-like tones” while preserving a photo’s “beautiful natural grain.”.

Recent findings suggest that the app supports Apple’s ProRAW and Basic processing, plus it can save photos as RAW DNG files for editing in other apps, like Darkroom, Lightroom, and Photoshop. It also supports HDR image capture across four settings: off, low, medium, and high.

Industry observers note that “!Camera is the first camera app to enable professional-level color grading with 3D LUTs (‘lookup tables’) used in high-end workflows by pro photographers to achieve realistic film simulations and unique cinematic looks,” Not Boring continues. The app includes photographer-designed LUTs, LUT importing, and preset creation tools. The company regularly releases new styles and collaborations.

Recent findings suggest that the app also packs extensive manual controls—including exposure, shutter speed, white balance, ISO, and focus—alongside tools like focus peaking, zebra stripes, and a histogram. For finer focus adjustments, the virtual lens features its own “Precision Focus Ring” with a focus scale.

Customization extends to the look of the camera app itself. Owners can design a custom virtual camera by choosing colors for its body, top panel, lens, and buttons.

If (Not Boring) Camera ultimately wins the award when winners are confirmed next month, it certainly won’t be the first camera app to earn the honor. In 2024, Kino and Adobe Lightroom were both honored among Apple’s Apps of the Year. Halide Mark II won in 2022, too.

Tech Report: Mexico's Parque del Jaguar protects jaguars with 18-kilometre limestone wall

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mexican studio Colectivo C733 has created an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through while protecting more than 1,000 hectares of forest at Parque del Jaguar in Tulum, Mexico.
  • The project aims to safeguard one of the region’s important habitats for jaguars, whose movement through the landscape had become disrupted by roads, development and tourism.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Rafael Gamo.

Mexican studio Colectivo C733 has created an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through while protecting more than 1,000 hectares of forest at Parque del Jaguar in Tulum, Mexico.

The project aims to safeguard one of the region’s important habitats for jaguars, whose movement through the landscape had become disrupted by roads, development and tourism.

Rather than creating a conventional enclosed nature reserve, Colectivo C733 designed a network of boundaries, access points and visitor facilities intended to protect the animals‘ habitat while allowing people to explore the area.

The park occupies a coastal territory containing tropical forest, mangroves, underground rivers and karstic geology, as well as the ancient Mayan archaeological site of Tulum.

Its landscape had also been affected by contaminated soil around a former airstrip and habitat disruption caused by the Cancún-Tulum highway.

At its perimeter, the studio added an 18-kilometre dry-stacked limestone wall, known locally as a tecorral, informed by traditional Mayan stone boundaries.

Built without mortar, the wall allows wildlife to move through gaps between the stones while establishing a physical boundary around the protected area.

Within the park, Colectivo C733 introduced a number of public buildings and viewing platforms, concentrating new construction in previously altered areas and leaving large sections of the territory untouched.

Low-impact transport routes, including pedestrian and cycling paths, connect the different areas, with electric transport also introduced to reduce the impact of visitor movement.

The routes link the park’s public facilities with its archaeological and ecological sites.

At the central entrance, a timber-framed building is screened by closely spaced vertical wooden members and topped with a woven palm-thatch roof.

The complex accommodates a museum, cafe, shop, multipurpose room and open-air forum, alongside a kitchen designed for cooking over smoke.

Other structures include elevated observation towers and a long suspended walkway that crosses the forest canopy, revealing different aspects of the area’s geology, water systems and biodiversity as visitors move through it.

“By designing how the territory is revealed, inhabited, and understood over time, Parque del Jaguar shifts architecture from a static intervention to an evolving framework that connects environment, culture, and collective awareness,” Colectivo C733 remarked.

Access is more controlled in sensitive areas, helping to limit disturbance to wildlife habitats, including those used by jaguars.

At the coast, stone platforms, stepped seating and raised timber staircases provide access to viewpoints overlooking the Caribbean Sea.

The buildings use locally sourced limestone, chicozapote timber, sascab – a naturally occurring limestone-based material – and palm thatch.

Green roofs, shaded outdoor spaces and naturally ventilated structures help reduce the need for mechanical cooling in the tropical climate.

Alongside the construction work, the project includes soil remediation, reforestation and the recovery of natural water systems.

Asphalt has been removed from previously developed areas as part of efforts to restore the ground and reconnect habitats.

Founded in 2019, Colectivo C733 brings together the practices of Gabriela Carrillo, Carlos Facio, José Amozurrutia, Eric Valdez and Israel Espín to work on public architecture and urban infrastructure across Mexico.

Its other projects featured on Dezeen include a square-shaped pedestrian pier that hovers over a lagoon in Bacalar, Mexico and a brick music school topped with a cantilevered coconut wood roof in Nacajuca, Mexico.

Photography by Rafael Gamo.

ITC Kabel brings angled terminals, an eccentric lowercase g, and a diagonally sliced e alternate that shaped Sugarsparkâs snaky S â while Herb Lubalin and Tom Carnaseâs Avant Garde Gothic anchors the uppercase W and tightly locking ligatures. On the 650pt ÃP poster and roller-skate ÃÃ specimen, neighboring capitals share stems and diagonals under solid-dot or hollow-ring umlauts.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, sotheby’s today confirmed that a settlement has been reached over the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890).
  • The Sotheby’s statement records that the auction house is “pleased to confirm that an agreement has been reached between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and all of the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer regarding the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs”.
  • In a recent development, the work is estimated at around $180m ($207m with fees) and has been guaranteed by Sotheby's to sell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sotheby’s today confirmed that a settlement has been reached over the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890). The work has been poised to achieve a record price for the artist but became the subject of a claim by the heirs of its Jewish former owners, who called for the work to be withdrawn from the 18 November auction in Newly introduced York.

The Sotheby’s statement records that the auction house is “pleased to confirm that an agreement has been reached between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and all of the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer regarding the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs”. The sale will now proceed as planned.

In a recent development, the work is estimated at around $180m ($207m with fees) and has been guaranteed by Sotheby's to sell. This is far in excess of the previous record of $117m, paid at Christie’s in 2022 for Van Gogh’s Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888).

The Blaquier-Arrieta family, from Argentina, bought Blossoming Chestnut Trees in 1975. As the Sotheby’s statement explains: “In recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement.”.

According to recent reports, the provenance in the Sotheby’s catalogue entry notes, as it has done since last month, that the painting was acquired by the Berlin publisher Samuel Fischer and his wife Hedwig in 1909. Their son-in-law, Gottfried Bermann Fischer, deposited the Van Gogh with the Amsterdam gallery Paul Cassirer in 1932 or 1933—and it was then bought by Paris collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in 1936.

Recent findings suggest that last Thursday (12 November), in a surprise move, the Berlin-based restitution researcher Gunnar Schnabel sent a letter to Sotheby’s, on behalf of the Fischer heirs. He questioned the 1936 sale—which he notes took place three months after the family had left Berlin for Vienna—asking Sotheby’s to prove that the picture had been sold at its market value and that its sale was not forced. In the meantime, Schnabel asked for this week’s sale to be delayed.

In a statement, the Fischer heirs commented: “We are grateful for the trusting and fair negotiation and collaboration with Sotheby’s and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which make it possible to acknowledge the suffering of the Fischer family during the Nazi era and honour Gisela Berman Fischer's [granddaughter of Samuel and Hedwig] history of seeking justice for her family.”.

In a recent development, the Blaquier-Arrieta family commented: “We are pleased to have reached an amicable resolution with the Fischer heirs. We appreciate the constructive dialogue that made this resolution possible and look forward to an extraordinary result and to passing along this masterpiece to a new generation of collectors.”.

No details have been released on the nature of the agreement and whether the Fischer family will receive financial compensation.

What impact, if any, the short-lived dispute will have on the sale will only become apparent with the bidding.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A couple of weeks ago, Jordan Drake texted me from the Lumix event in Osaka with the rundown on what was being announced.
  • Industry observers note that for context, this year is the 25th anniversary of the Lumix brand, and the firm opened with the L10 back in May.
  • And so I carried that excitement with me for the next six months, knowing we might not see that promise come to fruition until late fall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A couple of weeks ago, Jordan Drake texted me from the Lumix event in Osaka with the rundown on what was being announced. When he described the S1 II but in a box camera format, I couldn’t help but express my dismay. “That’s it?”.

Industry observers note that for context, this year is the 25th anniversary of the Lumix brand, and the firm opened with the L10 back in May. That felt like a proper start to what we assumed would be a full year of serious product introduces. This wasn’t an expectation we came in with; it was one that Lumix put into our heads: the company specifically said it had more planned for 2026 and that we should be excited.

And so I carried that excitement with me for the next six months, knowing we might not see that promise come to fruition until late fall. That is a major reason why I’m so disappointed by the SHX1. It’s not that the camera is bad or that it doesn’t have a core, dedicated audience. It’s more that this isn’t the camera that I was expecting to be the cap of a celebratory year where Lumix was poised to really strut its stuff.

Recent findings suggest that the Lumix S1H has been languishing for years, and not because there isn’t a market for it. It just seems like Panasonic doesn’t know what to do with it. When the S1 II was announced last year, that really felt like the case because the camera felt like it did everything we ever wanted the S1H successor to do.

Industry observers note that but I argue that, even with all that known, Lumix — the brand known for video performance — has, for some reason, been unwilling to take on Sony in the highly competitive commercial camera space that is dominated by the FX series. For all of its strengths in video, Lumix appears scared: either of Sony or of the success that would come from actually trying.

Recent findings suggest that in 2021, Sony announced the FX3 and, in one fell swoop, changed the game. It created the perfect camera for the mid- to high-end filmmaker at a really compelling sub-$4,000 price. It wasn’t part of the Alpha series, so Sony could fully focus on video performance. The FX3 is the logical conclusion to the success that the a7S series created, and it was (and still is) immensely popular.

As Jordan Drake put it in this week’s episode of The PetaPixel Podcast, the FX3 became the industry standard through its design.

Industry observers note that “It became just the industry standard for if you’re doing event work or commercial work. Because it is such a recognizable camera – like that gray, with that pronounced, sharp-edged grip – when producers and directors and people see it, they immediately know that’s acceptable. That’s the major thing I think Panasonic’s butting up against. An S1 II is every bit as capable but it looks like an old DSLR. And I think everybody wants to move away from that,” he says.

“The FX3 is just the visual language of a semi-professional small camera now.”.

Canon and Nikon got that memo, which is why the ZR and the R6V have that same visual design language. Panasonic Lumix has chosen to ignore that aspect of its cameras to its extreme detriment.

Industry observers note that compared to Sony, Panasonic’s camera division (it is now one division that combined Lumix and VariCam) is small, and maybe that’s to blame for these problems. Maybe it doesn’t have a good design department. That would make sense, since Lumix has not been a particularly good example of enticing camera design, and it’s very much hurting it now. I think it believes it should be able to stand out through performance alone, and that’s a lovely sentiment, but it’s just not reality.

Creators buy cameras that they want to be seen with, not just cameras that can do the job. You can argue that isn’t how it should be, but it is very much a reality.

Recent findings suggest that there is nothing wrong with the SHX1. It’s an excellent camera that will resonate with current Lumix filmmakers. Maybe that’s what Lumix wants: to keep its current audience happy.

Recent findings suggest that but that’s not what Lumix needs right now. To grow and find itself in more hands, Lumix needs to actually beat Sony at its own game – a game it is entirely equipped to win handily. I am a Lumix user and have been since the GH4. It’s reluctance to even try and take on the FX tier is incredibly disheartening, because I 100% would love to have an FX5-styled camera with Lumix guts.

Lumix’s in-body stabilization is better. Lumix’s record modes are, on the whole, better. I mean, the firm was giving filmmakers open gate and in-camera anamorphic desqueeze years before it was even a twinkle in the other brands’ eyes. This is the space where Lumix should be king, but its refusal to go at Sony head-on makes it seem like the company is scared it might not succeed.

In a recent development, or, worse, Lumix is scared of the success that would bring it. Maybe it doesn’t want that level of attention. Maybe it likes feeling like a scrappy underdog, and the idea of being a market leader is just too much pressure.

In a recent development, whatever the case, as good as the SHX1 is, it’s not the camera Lumix needed to release in this moment. Sony was stumbling and tripping over itself with the FX5 launch, giving Lumix the perfect window to jump ahead if it were prepared for the moment. It clearly was not.

I get not being able to directly respond to the FX5, but the FX3? Five years later, how do you not respond to that? You, the video camera manufacturer? It feels like cowardice despite the timing not possibly being any better… which makes missing that moment even worse.

Recent findings suggest that I don’t think Lumix fully grasps how badly they fumbled this opportunity. They might not realize the extent of this mistake for months or years. With the moment up for grabs, Lumix just chose not to reach out for it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fujifilm has revealed that it will host an X Summit in Paris on December 2 at 4 AM EST.
  • Recent findings suggest that “2026 is noted to mark 200 years since the invention of photography in France,” Fujifilm indicates.
  • Fujifilm has not hosted an X Summit in 2026, although it has hosted multiple Fujikina events around the world, including in Denmark and Poland this past spring and in New York City in October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fujifilm has revealed that it will host an X Summit in Paris on December 2 at 4 AM EST. X Summits have traditionally been Fujifilm’s stage for announcing a latest product, and given Fujifilm has not released an X-series camera this year, it could very much use one.

Recent findings suggest that “2026 is noted to mark 200 years since the invention of photography in France,” Fujifilm indicates. “To celebrate two centuries of photographic history, and to honor all the photographers and photography lovers who have created countless inspiring images along the way, the next X Summit comes to you from Paris, France.”.

Fujifilm has not hosted an X Summit in 2026, although it has hosted multiple Fujikina events around the world, including in Denmark and Poland this past spring and in New York City in October. The last X Summit was held in Shanghai in June 2025, which saw the announcement of the X-E5 and 23mm f/2.8 R. Before that, the X Summit in Prague rolled out the GFX100RF.

Going 18 months between X Summits is extremely unusual, but getting one in 2026 at all feels like a gift, given how quiet Fujifilm has been this year.

There is no official word on what to expect out of this X Summit (of course), although the perception has been that Fujifilm’s flagship cameras are in dire need of a refresh: the X-Pro, X-T, and X-H cameras are long in the tooth now.

Recent findings suggest that A new camera launch would also be an opportunity to address the largest complaint Fujifilm has come up against: autofocus. To its credit, Fujifilm knows it’s a place it must improve.

“We’re trying,” Yuji Igarashi, General Manager of Professional Imaging Group, Imaging Solutions Division, Fujifilm Corporation, explained to PetaPixel at CP+ 2026 in Yokohama. “We still believe it’s necessary to just continue to improve by algorithm improvement. And it’s not that we’re not doing it. We are continuing to work on it.”.

Speaking of future devices, Igarashi mentioned improved sensors and processors likely would help.

In a recent development, “In theory, future devices will be much more advanced, with the consideration of higher processing speed. That would help us as well, but that wouldn’t help existing people, so we’re trying to do both — algorithm improvement plus device improvement.”.

Fujifilm will broadcast the X Summit live on its YouTube channel on December 2 at 4 AM EST.

  • Named Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna, the project is nestled within a forest in Kanagawa, southwest of Tokyo, and forms part of the Daichi Silent River retreat alongside guest cabins and additional sauna spaces.
  • According to Daichi Inc, the idea for the project was to make the trees feel “part of the architecture itself”, using them as both supports and the defining feature of the pared-back structure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tree trunks puncture the slim timber platforms of this minimalist sauna in a Japanese woodland, designed by local architecture studio Daichi Inc.

Named Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna, the project is nestled within a forest in Kanagawa, southwest of Tokyo, and forms part of the Daichi Silent River retreat alongside guest cabins and additional sauna spaces.

According to Daichi Inc, the idea for the project was to make the trees feel “part of the architecture itself”, using them as both supports and the defining feature of the pared-back structure.

The sauna has been shortlisted in the Leisure and wellness category of Dezeen Awards 2026.

“Conventional architecture typically clears nature away, cutting down thick and strong trees and transforming them into standardised building materials,” remarked the studio.

“In this project, however, the existing trees were preserved and used directly as part of the spatial framework, blurring the boundary between nature and the built environment,” it added.

“Rather than placing architecture on top of nature, the project allows architecture to coexist with it, creating an immersive bodily experience in which people feel as though they are dissolving into the forest itself.”.

Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna’s structure comprises two stacked timber decks and a roof, with the central platform partially supported by the site’s natural slope.

The thin planes sit atop timber grids supported by the trees themselves and punctured by small circular cut-outs through which their trunks can grow.

Recent findings suggest that timber steps connect these different platforms, culminating on the upper level where the central sauna room sits, wrapped in frameless glass panels. It contains a wooden bench and a central log burner.

Aside from the sauna room and a small plunge pool, the decks are left entirely open and flexible, and are surrounded by slender metal balustrades at their edges.

“Wood and glass were used as the primary materials, while the existing trees themselves were integrated into the architectural framework,” noted the studio.

“Decks and sauna spaces were carefully positioned to appear as if floating within the forest,” it added. “The forest is not treated as a backdrop, but functions as an essential structural part of the architecture itself.

Other saunas recently featured on Dezeen include Puusauna in Finland by architect Jaakko Torvinen, which is supported by whole, charred tree trunks sourced from the neighbouring forest, and an off-grid bathhouse in London.

The camera, which has already earned a 2027 CES Innovation Award, features a custom Type 1/2 image sensor with Dual Native ISO and support for 4Kp60 and 1080p120 recording.

Obsbot notes the camera’s AI-powered image signal processing pipeline handles noise reduction and enables 4K HDR video at up to 30p with all-pixel phase-detect autofocus.

“All-pixel PDAF and Focus Over Zooming help the camera quickly refocus on distant, stationary subjects as focal length changes during a zoom,” Obsbot states.

Speaking of zooming, the Tail 2 ADV’s lens has an equivalent focal length range of 34-702mm and a variable aperture system. At the wide end, the aperture ranges from f/1.7 to f/7, while for telephoto shooting, it ranges from f/3.8 to f/7.

In Pro mode, camera operators can remotely adjust aperture, ISO, and shutter speed, offering greater creative control in changing lighting conditions such as stage performances, outdoor productions, and houses of worship.

In a recent development, the camera includes built-in subject recognition for autofocus tracking, identifying people, more than 30 animal species, and over 200 object categories. Using its pan, tilt, and zoom capabilities, it can automatically adjust framing to keep moving subjects in view. Operators can choose from six tracking speed settings alongside custom modes, as well as define preferred framing and tracking boundaries.

According to recent reports, “These settings allow live production teams to determine not just which subject the camera follows, but how it executes the shot,” Obsbot explains. The camera can also roll thanks to its built-in gimbal, enabling native 4Kp60 vertical recording without cropping.

For professional workflows, the Tail 2 ADV offers Obsbot Log—a proprietary logarithmic image profile that promises greater flexibility during color grading—alongside custom LUT support. Users can import and preview custom LUTs in Obsbot’s accompanying software, and the camera supports timecode and Precision Time Protocol (PTP) to sync with other cameras.

For connectivity, the Obsbot Tail 2 ADV includes 3G-SDI output up to 1080p60 and a full-size HDMI 2.0 output supporting up to 4K resolution. It also features Gigabit Ethernet, a 2.5mm RS-232 port, two USB-C ports, separate 3.5mm mic and line inputs, and a microSD card slot. The camera’s built-in 5,000mAh battery delivers over four and a half hours of operation, while USB PD 3.0 and PoE+ support allow for extended continuous power.

It has been revealed that the Obsbot Tail 2 ADV PTZR camera will arrive on December 8. Preorders are open now with a limited-time $200 discount, bringing the price down from its $1,599 MSRP to $1,399.

Harvard museum returns human remains to Brazil

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century.
  • In a recent development, the repatriation is part of a university initiative launched in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands.
  • The National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century. The remains were transferred from the collection of Harvard University’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

In a recent development, the repatriation is part of a university initiative launched in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands. The review identified one person who is recorded as having been enslaved, while there is strong evidence that the other was as well.

The National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology. According to records, it was obtained by Walter Hunnewell, a Harvard graduate who accompanied the naturalist Louis Agassiz on an expedition to Brazil in 1865-66, serving as the mission’s photographer.

Sources indicate that the skull was described in the records as the “skull of a negro”, with an accompanying note stating it had been “exhumed in the streets of Rio de Janeiro”, although circumstances surrounding its removal are still under investigation. The remains may have been taken from the Cemitério dos Pretos Novos, a burial ground in Rio used for enslaved Africans who died after arriving in Brazil that operated in the 18th century and early 19th century. The burial ground was rediscovered in 1996 during construction work in the city’s port district.

The Museu Nacional/UFRJ will assume temporary custody of the skull, which will not be publicly displayed nor used for research, reproduction or other purposes. Researchers will undertake further work to establish the woman’s origins before decisions are made about the skull’s final destination.

A ceremony on 11 November at the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro to mark repatriation of the remains of an enslaved woman from the Peabody Museum at Harvard University Courtesy Ministério das Relações Exteriores, Brazil.

Recent findings suggest that “This return represents a historical responsibility for the museum,” Juliana Sayão, the deputy director of the Museu Nacional/UFRJ, mentioned during the ceremony in Rio on 11 November. “We are confronted with the story of a person whose life was shaped by enslavement and the removal of her body from Brazil. Beyond assuming temporary custody, we are committed to treating this history with respect and responsibility.”.

Recent findings suggest that brazil’s minister of human rights and citizenship, Janine Mello, noted that the repatriation represents a milestone in acknowledging the historical violence resulting from enslavement. “The repatriation of human remains represents a fundamental step towards recognising the memory, history and dignity of the Black population of our country,” she remarked. “More than a century after they were taken from Brazil, these remains will return to the country to receive the dignified treatment to which they are entitled, in a process built on respect for memory, religious traditions and the communities involved.”.

Meanwhile, the Federal University of Bahia in Salvador received the remains of an enslaved African man of Nagô origin. The man is believed to have participated in the Malê Revolt in Salvador in January 1835, a major uprising led by both enslaved and freed Africans against slavery and religious persecution in Brazil. He was reportedly wounded during the uprising and subsequently died in hospital in Salvador.

A 2022 report on Harvard’s museum collections documented the presence of thousands of human remains, prompting scrutiny of how they had been collected and studied. Neither the museum nor the university returned The Art Newspaper’s requests for comment.

It has been revealed that more than four million enslaved Africans disembarked in Brazil during the transatlantic slave trade, making it the largest destination for the forced migration of Africans across the Atlantic. The country was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Instagram has introduced a upcoming feature that allows users to edit Stories after publishing them without losing existing views, likes, or replies.

Confirmed by Instagram head Adam Mosseri, the upgrade gives customers a 15-minute window to change text, music, stickers, and drawings after sharing a Story.

Previously, customers had to delete and repost a Story to correct a typo, change its caption, or add music they had forgotten to include. The latest feature removes that requirement, allowing edits to be made while preserving the post’s existing engagement.

In a recent development, the Verge notes that the ability to edit Stories was first spotted in development by reverse engineer Alessandro Paluzzi in April. It is now rolling out to users. To make changes, users can open a published Story, select the three-dot menu in the bottom-right corner, and tap “Edit Story.” Edited posts will display an “edited” label when viewed by others.

A post shared by Adam Mosseri (@mosseri).

In a recent development, the change also addresses some of the complications associated with deleting and reposting Stories, particularly when they form part of a sequence. Re-uploading content can disrupt the original order of posts, while creators and social media managers may also be concerned about the impact of reposting on engagement metrics.

“A lot of people have been asking for this, so I’m excited to get this one out there,” Mosseri says.

Alongside the editing feature, Instagram is introducing several changes to its Stories tools. These include new fonts, colors, and shapes for stickers, which will be organized into sticker sheets to make them easier to browse. The platform is also updating its multiple-photo selection process and adding new background options, including blur effects, colors and gradients.

Yesterday, PetaPixel reported on Instagram’s latest tool that’s designed to help creators on the platform protect their work.

Called content protection, it allows eligible creators to monitor copies of their videos across Instagram and Facebook and decide how to respond when a match is detected.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mexican design studio Arudeko has developed Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool, which can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.
  • Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.
  • The customisable textile – named Bianni – was made by weaving together wool with recycled paper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mexican design studio Arudeko has developed Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool, which can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

The customisable textile – named Bianni – was made by weaving together wool with recycled paper.

Skilled local artisans initially wove the discarded dyed wool onto a pedal loom, then, using cotton threads, wove strips of recycled paper crafted by local papermakers into the material.

The result is a translucent, flexible textile that can be crafted into diverse objects, from lampshades to decorative headboard panels, room dividers and wall art.

“Through exploring the material’s qualities, we discovered its potential, particularly the way light revealed colours that had been hidden within the paper, almost like a secret waiting to be uncovered,” Arudeko co-founder and CEO Denisse Arnaiz told Dezeen.

“Once the paper was woven, I began observing how it behaved as a textile,” added Arnaiz.

In a recent development, “Its translucency was what ultimately inspired us to explore its use in lighting. However, the material has many other possible applications.”.

With Bianni, Arudeko aimed to uncover the hidden value of discarded wool whilst reimagining the ancient material’s ancestral history and “cultural memory”.

Recent findings suggest that “Bianni was born from the idea of giving newly introduced life to the leftover wool from our rug and cushion production in Oaxaca,” said Arnaiz. “This wool carries within it the knowledge of the artisans who work with it, as well as the colours of the earth embedded in its fibres.”.

Arnaiz explained that the material is made purely from natural materials, with no additives.

“No additives, just natural materials – why mix these fibres?” she said. “Not only for an aesthetic purpose, as wool brings fire resistance to the paper.”.

In a recent development, throughout the process, the studio aimed to minimise water consumption and carbon dioxide production as much as possible. Bianni’s production was also kept local to reduce transport needs whilst supporting the local community.

By working with artisans from rural communities and blending traditional craft knowledge with contemporary design practice, Bianni aims to champion historic crafts whilst fostering long-term community development and economic inclusion.

Other wool projects recently featured on Dezeen include waste-wool cladding designed for retrofits and a collection of rugs with architectural designs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turner Duckworth rebuilt the Maker's Mark brand identity around its red wax, casting Star Hill Farm materials into marks that tell the story.

The bottle does the talking. Turner Duckworth kept the hand-dipped red top exactly where it belongs, at the center of the system, then built a whole language out of it. Wheat stalks, oak rings and native flora from Star Hill Farm were dipped and cast in the same red wax, so the marks that carry the brand are literal pieces of the place. Against a Wheat Cream ground, the red reads as one loud note in a quiet room, with Printmaker's Black holding the type steady.

In a recent development, the type comes from a person, not a library. Co-founder Margie Samuels shaped the original bottle, and the studio recreated her handwriting as a custom typeface with Nick Cooke at G-Type. Hundreds of characters, contextual alternates and ligatures keep it feeling handwritten rather than set, and her voice runs through the labels, menus and posters in a flowing, wax-like hand.

Sources indicate that layouts stay plain on purpose. A letterhead puts the Samuels family's SIV mark at the center and the distillery address in the corner, so place sits at the heart of every sheet. Type stays large and calm, with room around it, and the wordmark does its work without decoration.

The palette is the bottle, remembered in three tones. Wheat Cream is the ground, true to the label. Printmaker's Black carries the type. Wax Red does the rest, in finish and in form: powder-coated metal, glazing and varnish applied to objects with smooth, flowing shapes. The same red runs across mugs, folders, books and table tents, so every object in the world feels dipped from the same pot.

Recent findings suggest that scott Grummett photographed the world at Star Hill Farm in warm cream tones and natural light, with touches of glossy wax red. The pictures tell the slower story behind the liquid: hand-rotated barrels, hand-cut labels, hand-dipped bottles, and the land that gives it flavour.

Legendary Photographer Ellen Von Unwerth Says ‘There’s No Money Left in Fashion Photography’

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ellen von Unwerth, one of the most in-demand fashion photographers working today, says there is no money left in the industry today.
  • For more than four decades, Von Unwerth has remained one of the most influential figures in fashion photography, widely recognized for her bold and playful images of women.
  • However, in an interview with Fashion Network France, Von Unwerth has revealed how the resources allocated to fashion photography have dramatically changed and how the industry is no longer as lucrative as it once was.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ellen von Unwerth, one of the most in-demand fashion photographers working today, says there is no money left in the industry today.

For more than four decades, Von Unwerth has remained one of the most influential figures in fashion photography, widely recognized for her bold and playful images of women.

However, in an interview with Fashion Network France, Von Unwerth has revealed how the resources allocated to fashion photography have dramatically changed and how the industry is no longer as lucrative as it once was.

“These days, there’s no money left in fashion photography,” Von Unwerth tells Fashion Network France. “It’s nothing like it used to be, when there were 10 pages in magazines and newspapers, and posters everywhere. You don’t see that anymore. You don’t see the big billboards anymore.”.

Von Unwerth explains that fashion photography has become less financially rewarding as brands increasingly direct their budgets toward events and influencers rather than traditional print ad campaigns. She says photographers now face longer waits for payment, tighter deadlines, and less creative freedom than they had earlier in her career.

Recent findings suggest that “Now, the money goes into events, influencers… So there’s almost no money left,” she adds. “You have to wait a very long time to get paid. And then they want the photos tomorrow — or even yesterday! Before, we were on our own on set. It was really just us, the photographers. We were the bosses; we did our own thing. It was our kingdom; it was secret.”.

In a recent development, von Unwerth states fashion photographers have increasingly lost control over their shoots, with multiple behind-the-scenes [BTS] photographers and teams now working on the same set. She says this makes it difficult to establish who actually took a particular image once it is published. She compares modern fashion shoots to film productions, where a director oversees several camera operators rather than capturing everything themselves.

“Nowadays, there’s the BTS photographer. Then there are the BTS of the BTS. There are three other photographers doing different styles,” she tells Fashion Network France. “And I fought against that for a long time, but I’ve given up. Now there are five people taking pictures behind me. And you don’t know, when it comes out: “Is it my photo or is it someone else’s?” In the end, I just say it’s my photo! It’s like in the film industry: there’s a director, who oversees everything, and there are other cameramen filming.”.

Recalling a shoot for beauty brand L’Oréal, Von Unwerth says she became frustrated and ordered everyone to leave after discovering that around 50 people behind her were taking exactly the same photograph.

Von Unwerth’s comments come weeks after a report revealed that fashion photo studios are closing down as brands increasingly embrace AI thanks to the big savings offered by the technology.

Modigliani sculpture heads Phillips’s New York evening sale at $44.6m

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, robert Manley, Phillips’ chairman and worldwide head of Modern and contemporary art, noted in a statement that there had been strong bidding across Modern, post-war and contemporary art: “Nearly 90% of the works offered had never been previously sold at auction, with many of the sale’s works coming from esteemed private collections where they had been for decades.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A striking limestone head by Amedeo Modigliani sold for $44.6m (with fees) at Phillips Modern and contemporary evening sale last night (17 November), leading a nearly sold-out auction totalling $85.75m ($104.4m with fees). That is an increase of 55% from the same sale last November, which topped out at $54.8m ($67.3m with fees).

According to recent reports, robert Manley, Phillips’ chairman and worldwide head of Modern and contemporary art, noted in a statement that there had been strong bidding across Modern, post-war and contemporary art: “Nearly 90% of the works offered had never been previously sold at auction, with many of the sale’s works coming from esteemed private collections where they had been for decades. Tonight’s results are a powerful reminder that truly exceptional works continue to inspire extraordinary competition in the market.”.

Industry observers note that sales were brisk in a bustling room, the pace in part due to the large number of works backed by third party guarantees. With just 22 lots on offer—the house withdrew Derek Fordjour’s Haberdasher, estimated at $350,000 to $550,000, at the last minute—14 carried a guarantee.

It took less than a minute and a half, for instance, for auctioneer Henry Highley to hammer Claude Monet’s La Maison dans les roses (1925) at $3.2m, matching the $4m high estimate with fees.

Claude Monet's La Maison dans les roses.

Sources indicate that on the other hand, the Modigliani, also guaranteed, sparked a ten-minute three-way battle, escalating from the starting bid of $18m to $28m in just a few seconds before slowing to $100,000 increments. A phone bidder speaking with Phillips specialist India Phillips ultimately prevailed over clients on the line with specialists Jeremiah Evarts and Kevie Yang, placing the winning bid at $38.2m ($44.6m with fees) on an estimate of $28m to $35m.

The piece, dating from 1911 to 1912, is one of just 28 sculptures by the artist, and part of a larger series of limestone heads each titled Tête. The price, while impressive, failed to approach the $70.7m achieved by another work from the series at Sotheby’s Latest York in 2014, which remains the record for Modigliani sculptures. His painting record, $170.4m for the 1918 painting Nu couché—the sixth most expensive work ever to sell at auction—dates to the following year.

The evening’s second-biggest lot was David Hockney’s eight-panel oil painting David, Celia, Stephen and Ian, London 1982, which sold for $10m ($12.2m with fees) within its $10m to $15m estimate. The artist, who died in June at the age of 88, made the work in 1982. It reflects his experiments at the time with photographing a subject from slightly different, overlapping viewpoints to create Cubist-inspired collages, and marks Hockney’s return to painting after a period focused on photography.

Helen Frankenthaler's Seabreeze.

The painting, which was sold by the Joel and Carole Bernstein family collection, also boasts an impressive museum pedigree, including appearances at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, and the National Portrait Gallery in London.

In a recent development, rounding out the sale’s top three was Alexander Calder’s 1959 mobile Snow Flurry, May 14—one of the few works without a third-party guarantee, and being sold by the family of Brazilian art critic Mário Pedrosa. Yang caused some excitement when she raised her bid straight from $4.6m to $6m, a price no one else was willing to top. The total with fees was $7.5m, above a high estimate of $6m.

Industry observers note that helen Frankenthaler had the sale’s top result for a woman artist with Seabreeze (1980), which went for $4.5m (with fees). Frankenthaler followed that up a few lots later with Peacock Alley (1990) $2.7m (with fees), right in the middle of its $2m to $3m estimate.

Sources indicate that the night’s only bought-in lot was Anselm Kiefer’s Melancholia (2005), which carried an estimate of $650,000 to $850,000, but bidding stalled out at just $500,000. The rust-coated painting features a polyhedral glass-and-iron sculpture mounted on the canvas.

David Hockney's David, Celia, Stephen, Ian, London August 1982 (Four Friends) (1982).

And while Jackson Pollock’s 1946 abstraction Constellation did find a buyer, the work failed to meet its low estimate of $3.5m. Despite the current show of Pollock and his wife Lee Krasner uptown at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and a provenance boasting the legendary dealer Peggy Guggenheim, the work hammered at just $2.6m ($3.3m with fees). Frank Stella’s Port Tampa City, from the estate of the late dealer Robert Mnuchin, also hammered below estimate, at $2.8m ($3.5m with fees) despite an estimate of $3m to $5m. The orange canvas, in the shape of an eight-point star quilt block, dates to 1963.

It has been revealed that nevertheless, both paintings made the sale’s top ten list, slotting in at number eight for Stella and nine for Pollock, just above the second Frankenthaler. Other noteworthy results included Clyfford Still’s PH-589 (1959). Expected to sell for $4m to $6m, it hammered for $4.2m ($5.3m with fees) to an online bidder from Tel Aviv.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A trial over the long-disputed estate of Andy Warhol’s photographer Billy Name, including the rights to his extensive photo archive, finally begins this week.

Name became Warhol’s close collaborator and photographer in the 1960s. He lived in Warhol’s Fresh York studio, the Factory, for seven years and became the artist’s in-house photographer. Using a Pentax Camera, Name captured thousands of iconic photos of Warhol, his art, and the stars who visited the Factory.

His Factory-era photographs are regarded as some of the most important visual records of Warhol and the Pop Art movement.

However, when Name — who was born William George Linich — died in 2016, a legal dispute broke out over his estate, which included the rights to his valuable collection of photographs. More than a decade after Name’s death, the rights and fate of thousands of his photographs still remain legally contested.

Sources indicate that according to a report by Times Union, a latest jury trial at Ulster County Surrogate’s Court in Ulster County, New York, will finally decide who has the right to license the black-and-white photographs Name took of Warhol and who will control the future of his extensive photo archive. The case will be the first jury trial over an estate that Ulster County Surrogate’s Court has ever presided over.

It has been revealed that the dispute is between Name’s longtime friend and agent Dagon James and his niece Suzette Linich both of whom claim to be the photographer’s rightful heir. At the center of the legal battle are two different wills left by Name. Linich presented a will dated 2011 that named her as the executor and sole beneficiary of his estate. Although the court accepted the document, James subsequently presented a more recent will, signed in 2015, that left the entire estate to him.

It has been revealed that A key question in the trial is whether Name had the mental capacity to make the 2015 will. By 2014, the photographer, who is in his early 70s, was reportedly suffering from arthritis, diabetes, and depression and was frequently hospitalized. Name’s family argues that he was often confused and vulnerable to influence, alleging that James persuaded the photographer to exclude his relatives from his will.

Industry observers note that james disputes those claims, maintaining that Name was mentally competent, trusted him, and made a deliberate decision to leave him in charge of his photographic legacy. The attorney who prepared the 2015 will testified that Name had clearly expressed his intention to exclude his relatives from his estate and leave everything to James.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American bathroom brand Kohler has created Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet, through its spin-off venture, Kohler Health.

Dekoda is designed to be discreet and intuitive, clipping to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

In the emerging toilet-based health tracker market, it is the first device capable of blood detection, which it does through sensors developed at Kohler Health that identify haemoglobin.

The organization remarked the device is particularly useful for older individuals or those with chronic gut illnesses, who need to track their symptoms as part of their disease management programmes.

“When we developed Dekoda, our goal was to give people the tools to listen to their bodies, track meaningful results over time, and take charge of their own wellness journey,” mentioned Kohler Health managing director Nora Tophof.

“It’s notable to realise that the human eye is only capable of seeing so much – and trace amounts of blood or other problems are not always apparent,” she continued. “Subtle biological markers, such as microscopic blood or early signs of dehydration, often go unnoticed.”.

“Dekoda works quietly behind the scenes to capture those crucial clues, giving people clear, objective data they can use to help shape behaviours or share with their doctor,” Tophof mentioned.

People with dementia often forget to drink or lose the feeling of thirst, while people with gut diseases such as Crohn’s usually need to track their daily bowel symptoms.

A secondary target market is competitive athletes and fitness enthusiasts, who Kohler says can use the hydration data to make training adjustments.

According to recent reports, dekoda is compatible with most toilets. It has a simple flattened capsule shape in gleaming white polycarbonate and attaches to the outside of the rim with an adjustable clamp.

On the other side of the clamp, a customised camera points down into the bowl, using spectroscopy to detect the colour and consistency of urine and stool.

To withstand the bathroom environment, the exterior of the device is made of a polycarbonate that is antibacterial and chemical-resistant, while the mechanical components are made of stainless steel.

A specially trained algorithm analyses the collected data and insights are viewed in the accompanying Kohler Health app. It automatically tracks bathroom routines and identifies trends, while users can also add information about their meals, medications and exercise to add context, and share insights directly with their doctor when they desire.

Consumers’ data is encrypted as it travels between their devices and Kohler’s systems but decrypted and processed to provide the service.

Kohler Health remarked Dekoda, which was released in October 2025, is helping destigmatise the collection of gut health-related metrics, which individuals could previously only monitor through test strips or stool samples.

It is part of a small wave of new devices focused on analysing the body’s fluids, from spit to menstrual blood, as wellness technology expands beyond watch-style heart rate monitors and activity trackers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fine art photographer David Yarrow has sat down with Graham Bensinger for a long chat about his career and life.

Yarrow is one of the most commercially successful photographers working today. He’s probably best known for his dramatic, large-format black-and-white wildlife photographs, although he has moved into fashion, celebrity portraits, and staged scenes.

The Scottish photographer began his career in sports, covering the 1986 World Cup in Mexico for The Times of London, where he got a well-known shot of Diego Maradona holding the trophy aloft.

But as Yarrow tells Bensinger, he became disillusioned with sports photography after attending the Calgary Winter Olympics in 1988, fretting that it was too difficult to stand out from the many other photographers also covering events.

According to recent reports, so in his early 20s, Yarrow pivoted and moved into finance. On 9/11, he made some bold market moves minutes after the first plane hit the tower, netting him big bucks.

But Yarrow notes his finance career eventually fell apart when Bernie Madoff’s massive Ponzi scheme was uncovered, and investors pulled all their money out of his business.

If there’s one photo that put a rocket in Yarrow’s career, it’s the great white shark breaching while hunting a seal that he took off the coast of Cape Town, South Africa.

A post shared by David Yarrow Photography© (@davidyarrow).

According to recent reports, yarrow states he was with a picture agency at the time that sold it to newspapers and magazines around the world for him. It netted him roughly $16,000. The problem was Yarrow had spent $20,000 in the pursuit of that photo and so ultimately lost $4,000.

But redemption was on the way in the form of a Texas lawyer called “Jaws” who wanted to buy the great white photo. When Yarrow quoted $6,000, the lawyer couldn’t believe how cheap it was.

“That was my a-ha moment, or my road to Damascus moment, or when the penny dropped,” says Yarrow. “That was when [I realized] one person could pay me more for a photograph than all of the newspapers and magazines in the world.”.

Recent findings suggest that petaPixel covered Yarrow’s team portrait of the Norwegian soccer team on their way to the World Cup in the U.S. last summer. Yarrow got the team, which includes star striker Erling Haaland, to dress up in Viking gear.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The growing use of AI-generated food images in Japan, a country with strict laws against misleading product photography, is raising concerns.

Industry observers note that in much of the world, food photography on product packaging often exaggerates what is inside. But in Japan, it is illegal for companies to use misleading food photos on product packaging.

In Japan, food packaging must show the product exactly as it is even a tiny exaggeration is seen as misleading.

No fake ads. No chemicals. No adulteration. Just pure honesty in every bite. https://t.co/kFKP0n9a1c.

— Dr. Rajeshwari Iyer (@RajeshwariRW) October 28, 2025.

Japan enforces some of the world’s toughest packaging regulations. Companies must ensure that the photos on their packaging accurately reflect the actual product, and failing to do so can lead to legal consequences. Any discrepancy between a product’s image and the real item is considered misleading. Even minor exaggeration or embellishment can be treated as a violation.

Sources indicate that under Japanese law, photos on product packaging are treated as factual claims. If a photograph on a packet of crackers highlights toppings arranged in a certain way, the crackers inside must match that presentation. The size, shape, and appearance of the product should closely mirror what is depicted in the image.

However, despite Japan’s strict standards for product photography, AI-generated food images are rapidly spreading throughout the country’s food and restaurant industry, prompting a backlash from consumers, according to recent reports.

According to recent reports, an increasing number of food and beverage businesses are turning to generative AI to produce food images, menus, and promotional posters. The practice has frustrated some Japanese consumers, who say they deliberately avoid visiting restaurants that use AI-generated promotional images.

In one particularly example, a Japanese food truck went viral in the country after using AI images of a “tomato and scrambled egg rice bowl” that had a melted cheese pull look, despite the dish not having any cheese in it. Following online backlash, the food truck owner issued an apology and pledged to replace the AI images with real photographs.

Recent findings suggest that under current Japanese law, there is no requirement to disclose whether an image is AI-generated. However, in a country where the accuracy of product photography has long been subject to strict legal standards, the growing use of fake food imagery is raising questions about authenticity, consumer trust, and how far AI should be allowed to replace traditional photography and design.

Mecanoo transforms former gold vault into "city’s living room" in renovation of De Nederlandsche Bank in Amsterdam

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography is by Ossip van Duivenbode courtesy of De Nederlandsche Bank.
  • Dutch firm Mecanoo has completed a major renovation of the Netherlands’ central bank, which involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault.
  • The Francine Houben-led architecture studio oversaw a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation’s ugliest building.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography is by Ossip van Duivenbode courtesy of De Nederlandsche Bank.

Dutch firm Mecanoo has completed a major renovation of the Netherlands’ central bank, which involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault.

The Francine Houben-led architecture studio oversaw a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation’s ugliest building.

Located in the heart of Amsterdam, this huge concrete-slab building is in complete contrast to the city’s historic canal houses.

The original architect, Marius Frans Duintjer, had hoped to emulate the modernist works of Mies van der Rohe, but security requirements had resulted in “a fortress with fences, large boulders and armed military police,” according to Mecanoo.

The building was further complicated by later extensions, which included an extra storey above the low-rise main building and a cylindrical 14-storey tower built alongside the original central tower.

Mecanoo’s transformation was enabled by the relocation of gold reserves and banknote operations to a location in Zeist.

This allowed the architects to give the building a sense of transparency and openness that was envisioned from the outset, but had never been possible before now.

The project is an exemplar for sustainable renovation, as proven by its nomination for Dezeen Awards 2026.

Removing the cylindrical tower was pivotal, as it allowed space for a upcoming public garden at the heart of the scheme.

This tower was carefully dismantled, allowing many materials to be reused.

Salvaged concrete was used to build a upcoming quay beside the canal, while the rest was donated to social housing projects in the city.

The removal enabled a reorganisation of the ground floor.

The entrance was relocated to Frederiksplein, while floorplates were cut away to reveal the 61-metre-long former vault, which has been transformed into an exhibition gallery.

“The most secretive part of the bank is now its most public,” said Mecanoo.

“Inside the vault, visitors can immerse themselves in exhibitions and interactive games that tell the story of gold, money, the economy and DNB’s core activities.”.

According to recent reports, the retained structures were newly clad in red ceramic bricks. These incorporate the brown tiles that clad the building previously, with the old tiles crushed for use as pigment.

These combine with upcoming glazing, a Kastenfenster system of ventilated double-glazing with integrated sun shading, which has helped to reduce the building’s day-to-day energy requirements by an estimated 80 per cent.

Inside, the space linking the vault with the courtyard was designed as an indoor street, with seating areas along the edges and auditoriums (one formal, the other informal) at each end.

“Francine Houben’s inspiration came from the vibrant ‘street’ of the central hall in the former Faculty of Architecture building at TU Delft, which was destroyed by fire,” mentioned Mecanoo.

The rest of the building is organised into zones with varying levels of security.

A five-storey atrium organises the semi-public area, which includes a meeting centre and a restaurant overlooking the Singelgracht, while the more secure employee zones are located in both the courtyard building and the tower.

The meeting centre occupies what was previously a double-height cash hall, with distinctive tree-like columns.

The original spiral staircase still stands, alongside a second added by Mecanoo, while custom-designed tables feature integrated lamps.

Timber was used for many of the newly introduced surfaces, including a slatted ceiling made from locally felled poplar trees.

Shades of red, blue and orange extend across other surfaces and interior elements, including walls covered in recycled-plastic felt, carpets and furniture.

“The colour scheme is inspired by the vibrant paper currency from the last period of the Dutch guilder,” remarked Mecanoo.

The interiors are completed by DNB’s collection of artwork, energy-efficient lighting systems and circular planting boxes.

“The renovation transforms De Nederlandsche Bank from a closed fortress into a transparent circular landmark, repurposing the former gold vault as the city’s living room for the public,” concluded Mecanoo.

Other recent projects by the firm include the rock-like Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, the tile-clad Villa BW and the book-inspired Macau Central Library.
