💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in New York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.
  • It has been revealed that the hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees).
  • Thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in New York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.

It has been revealed that the hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees). The result was a marked improvement on last November’s equivalent sale, which made $390.1m, or $471.7m with fees.

Thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees. Three multi-million dollar offerings were withdrawn from the sale, including an Andy Warhol self portrait, estimated between $14m-$18m.

It wasn’t a perfect evening: six lots failed to sell. These included a small-scale group of seven Jackson Pollock paintings from the 1950s (est $7m-$9m); a 1915 Modigliani painting Beatrice Hastings sitting (est $5m-$7m); and a 1945 Léger canvas (est $1.2m-$1.8m). Including the three withdrawn lots, this amounted to an 88% sell through rate.

Still, six artist records were set, including the 11-ft high Fernando Botero bronze, Horse (2006), which was parked on the sidewalk in front of Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters, and made $4.2m ($5.2m with fees).

The marathon evening got off to a modest start with Mary Bauermeister’s wooden box construction packed with optical elements, Nature Mort (1967-69), which made $100,000 ($128,000 with fees), the first from the collection of investment banker and art scholar Herbert Lust.

The Lust trove of eight works (a Frank Stella estimated at $7m-$10m was withdrawn before the sale) realised $42m with fees, topped by Alberto Giacometti’s impossibly thin, 119cm-high bronze, Figure, demie grandeur (no.2) from 1949 that made $22m ($25.9m with fees), against an estimate of $20m-$30m.

Beyond Lust, a late and untitled Mark Rothko acrylic on paper laid down on canvas in fiery red hues from 1968 made $11.5m ($13.9m with fees) and Philip Guston’s feather light brush strokes in Painting from 1952 sold for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees), topping out the few Ab-Ex offerings.

It has been revealed that the evening featured two mega-priced lots, both estimated at $60m-$80m. Wassily Kandinsky’s Weimar-era abstraction Betonte Ecken (accentuated corners, 1923), which once owned by the Guggenheim Museum co-founder Hilla Rebay, soared to a record $74m ($85.8m with fees). The anonymous seller acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in May 1986 for $1m.

Sources indicate that gustav Klimt’s dazzling lakeside composition, Litzlbergkeller from 1915-16, was observed and painted by Klimt with the aid of a telescope positioned and capturing the stout likeness of the Austrian inn he frequented for eight idyllic summers. It floated to $71m ($82.3m with fees).

Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president, nabbed both works for anonymous clients on his rainmaking telephone.

The Klimt had been acquired by last night's consignor at Sotheby’s Latest York in May 1997 from the estate of Neue Galerie co-founder Serge Sabarsky for a then-record $14.4m.

It has been revealed that A standout of the season, Wilfredo Lam’s large, tropical-inspired composition executed in a Magical Realism style, Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l’herbe des dieux) from 1943, made a record $9.5m ($11.6m with fees). It debuted at the Pierre Matisse Gallery in 1944 and was recently featured in the Museum of Modern Art retrospective Wilfredo Lam: When I Don’t Sleep, I Dream. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s New York in November 1997 for $1.3m with fees. The Lam came to market backed by a third-party guarantee.

Industry observers note that impressionist era paintings were also in rich supply. Paul Cézanne’s luscious tabletop still life Tasse, verre et fruits (around 1877) was consigned by the 86-year-old billionaire businessman William I. Koch. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees).

The Cézanne was once owned by the former Dutch banker Siegfried Kramarsky, whose estate sold Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr Gachet from 1890 at Christie’s Upcoming York in May 1990 for a then-record $82.5m with fees.

According to recent reports, french painting masters continued with Camille Pissarro’s evocative and crowded Parisian cityscape (sans protesters), Le Pont-Neuf, après-midi de pluie, 1re série from 1901 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees). It last sold at Christie’s Fresh York in November 2019 for $6.5m with fees.

Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s Hercules and Achelous (1590).

Big name consignors were not in short supply as evidenced by a trove of Picassos and several Old Master works under the marketing title “Heroes & Lovers: Property of a Distinguished Collector”—also known as Jeff Koons.

The group was led by Picasso’s snogging couple, Le Baiser (October 1969), which is famed in part for its inclusion in the artist’s late paintings exhibition in Avignon at the Palais des Papes in 1970, and went for $26.5m ($31.1m with fees).

The monochrome composition depicting the artist and his wife and muse Jacqueline Roque conveys both passion and love in the artist’s last decade. Though a relatively significant price, it came nowhere near its $40-$60m estimate.

Backed by a third-party guarantee, the work was acquired by Koons from Sotheby’s Fresh York in May 2008 for $17.4m, the same year his Balloon flower-Magenta from 1995-2000 sold at Christies London for £12.9m, or $25.7m.

Picasso’s Tête de femme (Dora Maar), painted in wartime Paris on 25 May 1941 sold for $25.5m ($30m with fees). Another Dora Maar split-angle composition with her face featured alongside her rival Marie-Therese Walther from 1939-40 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees) against an unrealistic estimate of $10m-$15m.

Sources indicate that the Koons trove, backed by third party guarantees also included a trio of Old Master works, topped by Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s dramatic, mythological depiction of Hercules and Achelous from 1590, and hugely scaled at 91.45cm by 242.57cm. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees), below its $12m-$18m estimate but enough to once again set the artist's record. Koons acquired it at Christie’s Latest York in April 2008 for a then-record $8.1 million. All in, the Koons group tallied $104.7m with fees.

It has been revealed that willem de Kooning’s rushing Yellow River from 1958, deaccessioned by the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York “to benefit the collection", and once described by the late critic Thomas B. Hess as “abstract parkway landscapes”, made $9m ($11m with fees).

One of the best back stories of the season came courtesy of Georgia O’Keeffe’s Near Abiquiu, Newly introduced Mexico I (1930), which was found buried in a trunk by the niece of the East Village owner who received it as a college graduation present in 1963. Rarely does one see property titles from the East Village. One newspaper article said the elderly owner, a former Foreign Service member, decided to hide the painting away in the mid 1980s after one visitor eyed it and she grew suspicious.

It hasn’t been seen in public since 1931 when it was featured in Alfred Stieglitz’s An American Place gallery solo show of the artist. It made $3.9m ($4.8m with fees).

Another version of the curvy sand hills of the Rio Grande Valley composition where O’Keeffe had her studio sold at Christie’s Latest York in May 2018 from the collection of Peggy and David Rockefeller for $8.4m.

Though the Frida Kahlo painting Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (1952) was withdrawn at the 11th hour over export issues, her husband Diego Rivera fared better, with the floral Vendedora de flores, de Tehauntepec (1929) blossoming at $8.1m ($9.9m with fees). It blew past its $3.5m high estimate—another winner for the William I. Koch collection which all in realised $66.3m.

Industry observers note that “It felt like a very calibrated evening with a solid but measured pace,” mentioned Adrien Meyer, Christie’s auctioneer, as he exited the salesroom. “There was significant participation from Asia that I haven’t seen in a while.”.

The evening action resumes Wednesday at Sotheby’s and the awaited offering of a $180m Vincent van Gogh painting Châtaigniers en fleurs from 1890.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Canva has introduced latest settings that allow users to disable its generative AI features and reduce the amount of AI-generated material shown in its content library.
  • Industry observers note that the generative AI setting disables a range of tools, including Magic Expand, Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Layers, Magic Edit, Dream Lab, Canva Code, and AI Shapes.
  • According to recent reports, however, the change does not disable every AI-powered feature on the platform.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Canva has introduced latest settings that allow users to disable its generative AI features and reduce the amount of AI-generated material shown in its content library.

Industry observers note that the generative AI setting disables a range of tools, including Magic Expand, Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Layers, Magic Edit, Dream Lab, Canva Code, and AI Shapes. It also prevents users from generating images through Canva’s AI chatbot.

According to recent reports, however, the change does not disable every AI-powered feature on the platform. Tools such as Background Remover and Magic Grab will remain available, even when generative AI is switched off. Canva says these tools will stay enabled because they “make everyday tasks faster without generating anything new.”.

Sources indicate that the distinction is based on how the tools operate. While generative AI features create new content, Background Remover and Magic Grab work with existing images. The latter allows customers to select an object within an image and reposition it elsewhere in the design.

Sources indicate that A second setting allows people to reduce the amount of AI-generated material displayed in Canva’s content library. When enabled, the platform will prioritise human-created templates, graphics, and other design elements in search results.

Industry observers note that however, the setting does not guarantee that AI-generated content will be excluded entirely. Canva says that a “small portion” of its library consists of AI-generated material, and designs containing these elements will carry an AI label in their metadata.

Recent findings suggest that both settings can be accessed through the profile menu. To disable generative AI tools, consumers should go to Profile, select Settings, open Permissions, and switch off Enable generative AI features. To reduce AI-generated content in search results, they can navigate to Profile, Your Account, and AI Personalization, then enable the option to show less AI content.

It’s no secret that AI has a popularity problem, and Canva appears to be listening to that sentiment. Last month, PetaPixel reported that the manufacturer released an image generation model that wasn’t trained on photographs.

#57065. Breaking: How Close Can an Arri-Powered Phone Get to an Alexa Cinema Camera?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1808 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Petapixel ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: How Close Can an Arri-Powered Phone Get to an Alexa Cinema Camera?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1808 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that that Honor and Arri are now partners is old news, but putting the latter’s Hollywood-style color science into a smartphone is the more intriguing proposition.
  • Industry observers note that the phone itself, the Magic9 Pro Max, features headline specs like a dual 200-megapixel camera system, a dedicated imaging chip, and a monster battery.
  • A full review focusing on still photography is forthcoming, but I visited Arri’s studio in Burbank, CA, in October 2026 to see how it helped shape the way the Magic9 Pro Max renders video.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that that Honor and Arri are now partners is old news, but putting the latter’s Hollywood-style color science into a smartphone is the more intriguing proposition. The Munich-based company seems like an unusual collaborator for Honor, the smallest of the five major Chinese phone brands.

Industry observers note that the phone itself, the Magic9 Pro Max, features headline specs like a dual 200-megapixel camera system, a dedicated imaging chip, and a monster battery. A more substantive addition is the phone’s Arri Cinema mode, inspired by Arri’s Alexa cinema cameras, which we’ve already seen in the Honor Robot Phone. This presents an entirely different way to capture video on Honor’s flagship.

A full review focusing on still photography is forthcoming, but I visited Arri’s studio in Burbank, CA, in October 2026 to see how it helped shape the way the Magic9 Pro Max renders video.

Arri’s history in analog cinema laid the foundation for its color expertise, though early on, the company essentially carried someone else’s color science since the film stock itself determined the look. Arri’s film scanner and film recorder, the Arri Scan and Arri Laser, became fixtures in studios, where engineers learned “what makes film look like film.”.

Industry observers note that moving to digital cameras enabled Arri to study many different film stocks to build a single default look, supported by a logarithmic brightness curve and a custom color gamut. Thus came the “digital negative,” a flat, data-rich image meant for grading rather than direct viewing.

Recent findings suggest that with skin tones as a central design goal, the manufacturer claims it photographed many faces to build a gamut that could consistently render varied complexions. That also means more stable color science when footage is over- or underexposed, with shadows that don’t veer into purple territory. This reflects years of feedback from colorists on how quickly they could achieve a finished look with Arri footage.

For Honor’s part, this marks a first in that it was one of the only Chinese phone brands (along with Huawei) that, until now, hadn’t partnered with a European imaging brand. While not terrible, its previous flagships couldn’t produce the kind of video quality competitors were delivering. Partnering with Arri isn’t just about catching up, but about ultimately surpassing every competitor, including the iPhone.

Honor handles the pipeline, which is why its own H1 chip is an integral hardware piece. That chip works in the RAW domain for what it calls “lossless noise reduction and extra dynamic range.” Achieving “cinema-grade” dynamic range requires capabilities beyond what a standard mobile processor offers, which is why this dedicated silicon works in tandem with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset. Honor reps were coy about how this particular marriage actually works under the hood.

What we do know is that Honor’s team in France worked closely with Arri in Munich, which helped tune the image signal processor (ISP) by sending weekly software revisions during development. Beyond that, Arri personnel made no contributions to the phone’s hardware design.

It has been revealed that here’s what Arri has to work with in the Honor Magic9 Pro Max: The dual 200-megapixel main (24mm equivalent) and telephoto (85mm equivalent) cameras both have CIPA 8-rated stabilization. Arri Cinema mode records up to 4K at 60fps, supports a 2.39:1 or 16:9 aspect ratio, and has a base Exposure Index of 160.

Industry observers note that exposure Index (EI) is similar to ISO, though it functions differently on cinema cameras. Arri cameras normally work at the base setting for optimal dynamic range, which isn’t how it works on a smartphone camera given the smaller image sensors. The base EI is the setting where the camera’s designers determined the sensor captures a fixed range of light most effectively, delivering the best possible dynamic range. In practical terms, that means the phone needs more light to hit its sweet spot than an Alexa would, which makes sense for a much smaller sensor. Honor and Arri have to pull this off by warding off noise when shooting at higher EI settings in dim scenes.

Arri Cinema mode can shoot in LogC3, the logarithmic encoding used in Arri cameras before the Alexa 35, including colors that approach the LogC3 gamut. Honor claims both the main and telephoto cameras track the LogC3 curve almost perfectly, marking a first for Arri, which had never matched multiple sensors in a single device before. But there’s also a catch to exactly how this works.

Sources indicate that showing charts that compared the phone’s response against a real Arri camera, Arri states the phone clips in the highlights because its sensor isn’t custom-designed like Arri’s own “expensive” ones. The sensors are also vastly different in size, making the phone’s dynamic range far more software-driven than it would be on an Arri camera.

Note that I only mentioned the main and telephoto cameras—because the Arri mode won’t work on the ultra-wide camera. Honor says it reluctantly left the lens out, citing vague time constraints since the partnership was only about six months old (at the time I visited). Rather than rush to get that out, it prefers to “get it right first” before committing to adding that lens. It’s just not clear whether that could happen through a software upgrade or in a future device, since the main and telephoto cameras each required custom curves and color matching.

My own take is that tuning a third camera may cost more money than time, and given that this is Arri’s first attempt without its own sensors, it leaves the ultra-wide as the odd lens out. Even so, a wider focal range isn’t unfamiliar territory for Arri, given that its Signature Prime line includes an 18mm lens, so we’ll have to wait and see.

Inside the Arri studio—on a newly built set with both an Alexa and a Magic9 Pro Max capturing the exact same scene—the side-by-side clips look surprisingly close.

Looking at the footage from both cameras later on my own computer monitor and on different phones or tablets, Arri’s clips offer better clarity and gradations in skin tones, but not by the margin I’d expect given how vastly different the two cameras are. It’s fair to say these results not only compete with the likes of Vivo and Oppo, but also fire a real warning shot at Apple. I’m no longer convinced the iPhone is the smartphone video king.

Recent findings suggest that both Arri and Honor point to how they shifted the phone’s color patches (open circles for where the phone started, solid for where it ended up) so its output lands near a real Arri camera. The default look matches Arri’s pre-Alexa 35 cameras, with 14 built-in LUTs that are always available in Arri Cinema mode out of the box.

Adding LUTs is easy, with a comically high 87 looks available directly from either Arri or Honor online, all assembled from the organization’s Arri Media post-production house. These range from black-and-white variants that emphasize different color channels to period film emulations, seasonal grades, beauty, and teal-and-orange looks—all of which also work in DaVinci Resolve. Some are over-the-top throwbacks that might only fit very specific use cases.

In a recent development, while the sheer level of choice is undeniably substantial, it can promptly become a mess once you bring them in. Assuming you add all 87, you have no way of rearranging, organizing, or deleting any. Before long, finding the one you’re looking for becomes an almost endless scroll. You can also freely import custom LUTs from other sources—including any LUT built with Arri’s color science—which only adds to the clutter. I pointed this out to Honor reps, who stated they will see about fixing it.

Recent findings suggest that despite the potential for overcrowding the mode, Arri Cinema is a huge upgrade over what Honor had before. I’ve come away impressed not just by the image quality, but also by the versatility of the included LUTs, which make recording almost anything look interesting. Adding a film-like aesthetic that doesn’t feel like a papered-on filter is a factor, but so is shooting in Log with manual controls for creative license. Excellent stabilization and built-in audio controls help the cause. Tapping the microphone icon offers five directional options: Standard, Long-range, Close-up, Voice isolation, and Voice boost. They’re actually better than I expected, though you can still use an external mic if you want.

It has been revealed that the mode offers 4K or 1080p at 24, 25, 30, 50, and 60fps. It also supports the APV 10-bit codec, which, despite some compatibility complications, remains a viable ProRes alternative (thanks to smaller file sizes) when running those files through DaVinci Resolve.

Industry observers note that notably missing is 120fps, which is restricted to the standard Video mode and carries a dubious connection to Arri given the vague assurances I received. It’s not at all clear whether Arri’s color science is sprinkled in here, though my eyes tell me it’s not. What’s especially head-scratching is that the standard Video mode locks 4K resolution to the Vibrant style. Switch to any other style, and resolution drops to 1080p for reasons I can’t ascertain. A software upgrade should easily fix that, but we’ll have to wait and see.

It’s key to remember a key distinction in defining Arri’s role, which is based on image science, not optics. Despite making lenses and accessories for its own cameras, Arri isn’t involved in what Honor is doing on the optical end at this stage. So, unlike Xiaomi and Leica, Vivo and Zeiss, or Oppo and Hasselblad—which routinely collaborate on lens hardware—that isn’t the case for the Magic9 Pro Max.

At its core, a cinema organization teaming up with a phone maker is a commercial play. Arri reps note that cinema remains the company’s priority, even as the market for high-end cinematography shrinks amid falling competitor prices. Licensing Arri’s color science is a way to reach people who may never buy a cinema camera while making them familiar with Arri Looks and post-production workflows.

Arri tried this before by collaborating with Panasonic on software upgrades, including for the Lumix S1R II, GH7, and GH6, where Arri certified Panasonic’s implementation of the LogC3 curve. A smartphone partnership, however, is far more mainstream and exposes the brand to a much wider audience.

Recent findings suggest that I asked if we might see these color science changes apply to Honor’s still photography as well, but both brands were noncommittal. Arri reps admit they have little experience in stills but would like to see it happen, whereas Honor declined to discuss any roadmaps on that front. It’s not clear if the two brands signed a long-term agreement, but from the looks of it, they blueprint to collaborate on more than just a few devices.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pentagram drew a full custom alphabet for Storefront Gala 2026, turning the Oyster Bar sign into loud, blocky, crayon-bright type.

Recent findings suggest that the gala took over the Grand Central Oyster Bar on September 28, honoring artist Mel Chin, arts leader Deana Haggag, and the architecture firm SO-IL. Anyone who has eaten under those Guastavino vaults knows the sign on the wall. Rudolph de Harak packed its letters tight, rimmed them in heavy black outlines, and filled them with colors straight out of a crayon box. Against wood paneling and old tile, it has always looked like the one guest in the room who came to have fun. Pentagram started from a simple question: what would the rest of that alphabet look like?

The answer is a custom display typeface with a full set of letters and numerals. Strokes run broad, corners clip short, and counters turn angular. The O is an octagon with a diamond punched through its middle, and that shape sets the rules for every other character. Blue, green, yellow, orange, red, and purple take turns filling the forms.

Storefront Gala 2026 appears in compact stacks and stepped arrangements, with rotated numerals adding an unexpected twist. Letters meet along their black outlines and lock into continuous compositions that feel assembled from colorful building blocks. A smaller sans serif organizes the event information around these expressive forms, holding the honorees, the venue, and the date in quiet lines above the noise.

The system runs across digital announcements, posters, a folded program, screen graphics, and embroidered caps. Some pieces set the colored letters on white, while others flood the ground with a single saturated color and let the type push back. The folded program carries the full stack in a run of blue, green, yellow, orange, red, and purple, with the small sans serif keeping the facts straight at the top of the sheet.

The caps are the most tactile piece of the set, the lettering stitched small across white, green, and pale blue cotton. An orange sign stands on the tiled floor, and the word SALOON stretches across a wood doorway in the same blocky letters, proof the alphabet holds its shape from a poster down to a doorway. Pentagram has designed identities for Storefront since 2012, and this one plays the longest with the room it was made for.

Photography by César Béjar.

A stepped facade fronts this pink commercial building in Mexico called Rosadoce, designed by local studio Reims 502 to suit various tenants over its lifespan.

Rosadoce is located in a low-density residential neighbourhood near the historic centre of Querétaro, a state in north-central Mexico, which is redeveloping into a mixed-use area.

The studio said the 840-square-metre building was “conceived as an adaptable urban asset” that can function as a single unit, four independent commercial spaces or sixteen smaller modules, ensuring its longevity and usability well into the future.

“Rosadoce by Reims 502 is a flexible commercial building in Querétaro, Mexico, designed as an adaptable urban platform for work, commerce and public life,” mentioned the studio.

“Designed during the pandemic, it rethinks commercial architecture in response to changing patterns of work, consumption and urban life.”.

Local planning constraints determined the building’s scale, while its “non-referential form” evolved from various design strategies, the studio said.

It reaches seven metres in height – the maximum height allowed above street level – which led the studio to carve out a semi-basement level to increase usable area.

Above ground are two open-plan levels, organised around a central stair and punctured by vertical voids that naturally light and ventilate the building.

Meanwhile, the basement currently contains service spaces including parking and plant rooms. However, similarly to the rest of the building, it has an open-plan layout to support future commercial activity.

Crowning Rosadoce is a usable rooftop filled with planters that provide thermal insulation.

Recent findings suggest that rosadoce’s distinct front elevation is formed from a series of staggered openings, described by the studio as evoking an “inverted stair”. This allows in light and ventilation while maintaining privacy.

“The inverted-stair facade creates horizontal openings for daylight and views while regulating visual permeability from the street,” remarked the studio.

“Because the building’s future uses remain open-ended, the facade avoids excessive transparency and provides a controlled threshold between public exposure and interior flexibility.”.

The pink render that colours the building’s exterior, provided by lime-based products manufacturer Nanocal, was chosen as a nod to the rose-colored quarry stone that defines Querétaro’s historic centre.

This same colour was used throughout the project, with the steel structure, concrete blockwork, grilles and service equipment all finished in the same tone, creating a warm feel for the interior.

According to the studio, the building’s future flexibility is achieved through the combination of open plans as well as “exposed construction, passive environmental strategies and an active rooftop”.

“This allows it to respond to different economic scenarios, tenant profiles, subletting arrangements and future programmes without major structural alterations,” said Reims 502.

The project is on the eight-strong shortlist for the small workplace interior category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards.

Other pink buildings in Mexico include a co-living apartment block with a series of arched forms by Estudio Zero and a minimalist house sandwiched between two buildings by César Béjar Studio.

Photography by César Béjar.

Latest Update: Della Robbia relief at the Frick Collection gets a crucial upgrade

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For a good part of the 15th and 16th centuries, Florentine sculptors named Della Robbia were making glazed terracotta works of great renown.
  • “We’re suggesting it’s by Andrea,” notes Greta Llanes Serrano, a conservation fellow at the Frick who worked on the recent treatment that helped pinpoint the newly introduced attribution.
  • It has been revealed that the framed relief depicts a veiled Madonna holding a Christ child, attended by cherubs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a good part of the 15th and 16th centuries, Florentine sculptors named Della Robbia were making glazed terracotta works of great renown. But not all Della Robbias were created equal. Scholars and collectors have long given strong preference to Luca della Robbia (1399/1400-1482), the founder of the dynasty, and his nephew Andrea della Robbia (1435-1525). Similar works by later Della Robbias and those produced by the workshop can come in a very distant third. For decades, Latest York’s Frick Collection believed it owned a relief by the family workshop, dated no earlier than the 16th century. But now, after technical analysis and consultation with experts in the field, the museum has updated its Virgin and Child to a 15th-century original, likely from the 1470s or 80s.

“We’re suggesting it’s by Andrea,” notes Greta Llanes Serrano, a conservation fellow at the Frick who worked on the recent treatment that helped pinpoint the newly introduced attribution.

It has been revealed that the framed relief depicts a veiled Madonna holding a Christ child, attended by cherubs. Fashioned out of buff-coloured earthenware, it has the Della Robbia clan’s distinctive white and blue glazes, with, in this case, traces of gilding. The work was first acquired by Helen Clay Frick, Henry’s daughter, in 1922 and spent most of the last century stashed outside the main reading room of the Frick Art Research Library.

Greta Llanes Serrano treating the Frick's Della Robbia in the Frick Collection's newly built Sherman Fairchild Center for Art Conservation Photo: George Koelle.

Llanes Serrano claims the road to the new attribution was filled with twists and turns, and an outright gap or two.

In a recent development, the early American luminary in Della Robbia studies was the Princeton University art historian Allan Marquand (1853-1924). Llanes Serrano says that in a 1906 publication Marquand identified the work, then in the possession of a private German collector, as being by either Luca or “very early Andrea”. Then, in 1914, he decided “that it had to be Andrea”. After it landed in the Frick family collection and found its way to the library entrance, it went from being a Della Robbia, generally, she says, to a work by Andrea—a decision, she notes, recorded by a librarian, though who actually made the decision is not known. Later, it was outright demoted to “school of Della Robbia” and has had that lower-rung status since at least 2008.

Julia Day, who was appointed last year as the Frick’s fresh chief conservator, thought it was time to take a new look at the work after attending a Della Robbia conference in spring 2025. “I just thought that we have this piece, and nobody’s really spent time looking at it,” Day claims.

According to recent reports, llanes Serrano, who analysed the relief over the last year in the Frick’s upcoming conservation studio, indicates XRF analysisallowed her to move back the dating and place it closer to Andrea himself. “I took multiple readings on different spots on the back and front,” she says, of the non-invasive technique.

Greta Llanes Serrano treating the frame of the Frick's Della Robbia in the Frick Collection's newly built Sherman Fairchild Center for Art Conservation Photo: George Koelle.

According to recent reports, the process revealed the elements present in the glaze, and then she compared her results with other analyses of autograph Della Robbia works. This helped her to place it in the new 1470s-80s time frame, when the older Luca was giving way to the younger Andrea. Meanwhile, another clue was plainly visible: “The Christ Child is clothed,” she says. In later versions of the motif made by the sculptors and their workshop, she adds, it was more common to show him unclothed.

A few weeks ago, the museum moved the work away from the library, where it was out of view from the general public, and installed it in a damask-lined spot in the mansion’s first-floor Octagon Room, fresh from its makeover during the Frick’s recent renovation.

Day says this kind of conservation-guided upgrade is a rarity at the Frick, happening perhaps once a decade. The Virgin and Child is the only Della Robbia piece in the museum's collection, she adds.

Breaking: The Filmmakers Behind ‘Primetime’ Printed the Entire Movie on 16mm and Rescanned It

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Primetime, a feature film about Chris Hansen and his hit TV show To Catch a Predator, keeps viewers gripped not just by the intense story brought to life by actors Robert Pattinson and Merritt Wever, but by the striking cinematography.
  • One of the biggest reasons for its distinct filmic look is that director Lance Oppenheim and cinematographer David Bolen opted to shoot the majority of the movie on an Alexa 35 before printing it onto a 16mm Kodak 50D and rescanning it to 6K, a process known as digital-to-film-to-digital.
  • Writing for American Cinematographer, Bolen explains that he shot most of the film at 6400 ISO to “add as much noise and texture as I could.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Primetime, a feature film about Chris Hansen and his hit TV show To Catch a Predator, keeps viewers gripped not just by the intense story brought to life by actors Robert Pattinson and Merritt Wever, but by the striking cinematography.

One of the biggest reasons for its distinct filmic look is that director Lance Oppenheim and cinematographer David Bolen opted to shoot the majority of the movie on an Alexa 35 before printing it onto a 16mm Kodak 50D and rescanning it to 6K, a process known as digital-to-film-to-digital.

Writing for American Cinematographer, Bolen explains that he shot most of the film at 6400 ISO to “add as much noise and texture as I could.”.

According to recent reports, the crew used London-based Cinelab, which has a third-generation 16mm Cine-Mitchell recorder built in-house. Once the film print was created, it was scanned back into digital using an Arriscan, which delivers “perfect edge-to-edge focus.” The resulting footage was then regraded.

Industry observers note that “Primetime is also a period film, in a way, and working with the film print helped make the visuals far more immersive,” notes Bolen. “Any feeling of artifice in the image seemed to disappear after printing to film.”.

However, the film wasn’t shot entirely with the digital-to-film-to-digital method: Oppenheim and Bolen utilized a few obscure, frankly bizarre, cameras as they searched for a way to recreate that early 2000s aesthetic and also communicate the plot to the audience.

Sources indicate that one such camera was a 2005 MiniDV camera, the Panasonic AG DVX 100B. Bolen used this for the hidden camera shots, and it is a very similar technology that was used to film the original show, To Catch a Predator.

According to recent reports, “These cameras are a challenge, because unlike modern cinema cameras, they can’t shoot in a LOG color space,” Bolen states. “We didn’t really alter their baseline settings; we decided to lean into the cameras’ built-in contrast. To Catch a Predator has such a strong look, and we tried to match it as closely as possible in-camera. Even in the final grade, we made very few adjustments.”.

But that distinct look posed a problem in the editing room: how to blend the shots taken by different cameras together. After all, DV cameras are not cinematic.

“We couldn’t get them to match,” indicates Bolen on the Mark Bone YouTube channel. “Like, no matter what we did with the settings, some would skew red, some would skew green, on some the exposure seemed off.”.

It has been revealed that but Oppenheim didn’t care and threw the rules out of the window. In fact, he would film the same scenes on different cameras, and then in the edit, choose whichever one he liked.

Speaking of other cameras, there were two more that Oppenheim and Bolen used: a Plumbicon tube camera and a medical camera — the kind used for colonoscopies.

Archer Green points out that the Plumbicon tube camera actually dates back to the 1980s.

It has been revealed that “It was meant to serve as a ‘spiritual’ camera rather than a period-accurate one,” Bolen writes for American Cinematographer. “These cameras use vacuum RGB tubes that split light into red, green, and blue, and the beautiful thing is that the tubes age and burn out over time. In a way, it’s a camera that feels like it has a soul — it decays over time, just like a human does.”.

The creators of ‘PRIMETIME’ explain how they shot a scene using a 480p colonoscopy camera 🎥🤯https://t.co/Z8m4aT7YM0.

— Complex Pop Culture (@ComplexPop) September 27, 2026.

Industry observers note that for one of the close-ups of Pattinson, Bolen used a doctor’s colonoscopy camera. The crew even built a rig to hammer home the effect.

“That was a scary one because that camera does shoot 480p and I was like, ‘How am I going to get this approved?’ But to A24’s credit [the film distributor], they were like, ‘this is awesome’,” Bolen indicates.

“There are no rules. We don’t have to shoot 6K. 480p looks awesome on the substantial screen; I love it. It’s my favorite part of the movie.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Halide has announced version 3.4, much of which focuses on optimizations for the iPhone Duo. This includes a latest “XL” mode that is designed for two-handed operation, as well as a feature that doesn’t avoid the crease, but instead embraces it.

Version 3.4, which is available starting today, promises to maximize the viewfinder when the iPhone Duo is unfolded. Halide notes this feature, called XL mode, allows for “powerful two-handed operation.”.

“On the outer screen, we’ve added a few new modes, including a viewfinder preview and flash-fill. In low-light, the latter gives you a softer alternative to the built-in flash,” Halide adds.

“While apps like Apple’s own camera app expand the viewfinder to take up the full screen, it’s impossible to do this without obstructing your shot with camera controls. That poses a challenge when composing shots, so we’ve taken the approach of keeping the viewfinder clean.”.

Beyond just making these changes that take advantage of the two form factors the Duo offers, Halide went one step further and specifically engineered an interface for when the Duo is half-folded. The firm says that while most are avoiding the crease that appears when the phone is folded, it went the opposite way and embraced it.

“Back when the iPhone X launched in 2017, we were the first app to ’embraced the notch’ by putting histograms in the ears of the phone. Today, we think we’re the first app to ’embrace the crease,’ placing the histograms in the fold, an otherwise no-man’s-land of interactions,” Halide indicates.

By default, Halide’s camera controls sit on the same side as the camera itself. Tapping the arrows in the sidebar, the left and right sides swap, turning Halide into a waist level viewfinder.

Halide provided a few sample images taken with the updated Duo app:.

Recent findings suggest that halide usually doesn’t take long to patch its app when latest hardware lands, and even though the interface for this Duo-specific update feels like it should have taken a lot longer, it really isn’t too far off from what Halide provided for Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro launch. When it dropped version 3.2, which gave support for variable aperture control, that arrived on October 2, which is about three weeks after the iPhone 18 Pro landed on store shelves. This update for the Duo comes just shy of a month after the Duo launched on October 23.

Halide version 3.4 is available starting today.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Local practice Tant A Temps Design aimed to revive the aesthetics of the Tang Dynasty when designing the interiors for cafe Laibei 1087, located in a historical building in Xi’an, China.
  • The cafe sits inside the Beilin Museum, originally constructed in 1087 to preserve stone steles inscribed with Confucian philosophy and famous calligraphic works.
  • The timber columns and beams of the historic building were preserved, with the same approach extended into the cafe interiors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Xiao Tan.

Local practice Tant A Temps Design aimed to revive the aesthetics of the Tang Dynasty when designing the interiors for cafe Laibei 1087, located in a historical building in Xi’an, China.

The cafe sits inside the Beilin Museum, originally constructed in 1087 to preserve stone steles inscribed with Confucian philosophy and famous calligraphic works.

The timber columns and beams of the historic building were preserved, with the same approach extended into the cafe interiors.

Guided by a “minimum intervention” and “zero damage” renovation strategy, Tant A Temps Design made every new addition detachable and reversible, which allowed the building’s original features to remain untouched.

In the cafe, the furniture is suspended from wooden beams or arranged around columns to avoid direct contact with the original structures.

Tant A Temps Design also created tables, chairs and display cabinets with designs that draw from elements of the ancient building framework, such as the beams, columns and dougong brackets.

Lightweight and prefabricated materials and modular systems were used throughout the space.

For the main colour palette, Tant A Temps Design chose light green hues complemented by gold accents.

“The purpose of choosing this colour scheme is to restore the visual characteristics of Tang architecture – robust, imposing and richly coloured,” the studio explained.

“Abandoning the rigid replication of ancient architecture, it extracts and reshapes the spiritual core of Tang and Song aesthetics through a restrained colour palette and minimalist structural language, creating a serene and elegant atmosphere that highly matches the cultural temperament of the Stele Forest.”.

An integrated functional island was designed to function as the central bar counter.

All modern utility systems, including air conditioning, water, electricity, lighting and exhausts, were concealed and integrated into the top and bottom of the bar counter.

This is consistent with the studio’s commitment to preserving the heritage building while giving it a contemporary, functional upgrade.

“This forms a functional system that is both independent of the original building structure and seamlessly integrated into the historical environment, setting a newly introduced paradigm for the adaptive reuse of similar cultural heritage buildings,” remarked the studio.

The cafe is part of a 220-square-metre development that also includes a rest area, a retail zone and a stone-rubbing workshop that serves as a history learning centre.

According to Tant A Temps Design, the project has transformed a dormant historical building into an accessible and interactive cultural space.

Led by founder Wei Chen, Tant A Temps Design is an interior design practice based in Xi’an.

Elsewhere in China, Linehouse has completed the interiors of the Jen hotel in Hangzhou and Keiji Ashizawa designed an “open and inviting retail space” in the historic building in Shanghai.

Photography by Xiao Tan.

ACDSee Photo Studio has confirmed version 27, which brings a bunch of newly introduced features, including several powered by AI, perhaps elevating the tool to the level of Adobe’s offerings.

Version 27 of the photo management and editing software for macOS introduces generative AI tools for creating and editing images, along with AI-powered organization that the company states can find and group photos together by how they look. These new options don’t compromise non-destructive editing, either.

In short, ACDSee has embraced AI editing.

“AI is shaping the future of photography and it’s our goal to lead the way in that space,” Frank Lin, CTO of ACD Systems, states. “With ACDSee Photo Studio for Mac 27, we’re bringing generative AI directly into the creative process, making it easier to find, organize and transform images while giving photographers the flexibility and control they need to bring their vision to life.”.

The bulk of the updates to version 27 are AI-focused, with the top-billed fresh feature having the highest chance of being the most controversial: image generation.

“Turn a text prompt into an image, choose a preset visual effect, or bring in reference images to guide character, style, and composition, right inside the photo workflow,” ACDSee says. AI generation isn’t upcoming for photography tools, as Photoshop has had it for years now, but it’s not necessarily something that photographers are specifically asking for in a Lightroom competitor. Still, it’s here now.

ACDSee appears to be following Adobe’s lead with the next feature, as it now supports editing via prompting. Photographers can describe a change in plain language or “use reference images to guide the look, and reshape a photo without a single brush stroke.”.

The AI search tool looks to be an alternative to Excire Photo and will find photos visually related to any primary target, with no keywords or tagging required. Images can also be grouped by similarity.

ACDSee Photo Studio for Mac 27 is available for $119.99, including 10,000 AI Credits for generative AI tools and 100GB of cloud storage.

Inside its dark floating interface, team members smear harmful social imagery using an intensity slider, toggle between Kometa and Spezia Serif, and export ready-made compositions.

That filtered blur doesnât stay trapped in a digital sandbox. It smears into horizontal red and teal bands behind âSAVE SOCIAL FROM MEDIAâ on a corrugated building billboard and softens a framed âDONâT LET LIKES REPLACE LOVEâ poster. Across Instagram Stories, itâs paired with candid portraits and an acid-green âSAY BYE TO SUBSTANTIAL TECHâ card. On the events module, solid green, cobalt, and charcoal blocks sort talks with Jonathan Haidt and Daniel Gilbert into clean typographic columns. According to OMSE, the visual identity helped B416 secure nationwide campaign funding, cross its 45,000-signature target, and push the Latest Zealand Government to introduce a Bill setting a social media age limit.

Breaking: Ten essential artworks to see in Budapest

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in April, Hungarians shook off 16 years of right-wing populist rule when they voted overwhelmingly against prime minister Victor Orbán and his Fidesz party.
  • According to recent reports, hungarians trace their history back to around 900 AD, when nomadic Magyar tribes arrived in Europe’s Carpathian basin, but their capital city and their national identity are really 19th century inventions.
  • Industry observers note that hungary’s best-known art institution, the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest (MFAB), first opened in 1906 on the Pest side of the Danube, though it has roots in an earlier collecting spree of the Esterházy family, the highest of Hungary’s high nobility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in April, Hungarians shook off 16 years of right-wing populist rule when they voted overwhelmingly against prime minister Victor Orbán and his Fidesz party. With Orbán’s culturally regressive movement in tatters, Budapest is now reclaiming its status as one of Europe’s most crucial artistic capitals, and experiencing a wave of visitors newly drawn to the city in the wake of the country’s political about-face.

According to recent reports, hungarians trace their history back to around 900 AD, when nomadic Magyar tribes arrived in Europe’s Carpathian basin, but their capital city and their national identity are really 19th century inventions. The sprawling, multi-ethnic Kingdom of Hungary, which once stretched from the Mediterranean to what is now southwestern Ukraine, rebelled against Hapsburg dominance in the mid-19th century. That break culminated in 1866, when Austria and Hungary became constituent parts of a newly introduced dual monarchy, spurring on the 1873 union of the separate towns of Buda and Pest, reconstituted as a Belle-Époque boomtown.

Industry observers note that hungary’s best-known art institution, the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest (MFAB), first opened in 1906 on the Pest side of the Danube, though it has roots in an earlier collecting spree of the Esterházy family, the highest of Hungary’s high nobility. The museum’s broad range of Old Master paintings and its world-class prints and drawings collection arguably make it the most key museum of its kind between Vienna and St. Petersburg. In 1957, the bulk of its Hungarian holdings were separated into a new institution, the Hungarian National Gallery, which eventually moved over to the Buda side of the city, into the onetime Habsburg Royal Palace. Though the Orbán regime had planned to rehouse it again, it remains in situ for the time being, and its collections of Hungarian art, spanning centuries, testifies to a rich and varied artistic tradition almost entirely unknown outside the country. Back over in Pest, a new cultural development, Müpa Budapest, opened in 2005, providing a home to the city’s Ludwig Museum, with a collection of contemporary art from national and international figures.

Raphael's Esterházy Madonna (around 1508).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Raphael's Esterházy Madonna (around 1508)Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareTiny and technically unfinished, with the Virgin’s face and the figures of the Christ child and St. John the Baptist mere underdrawings, this tempera-and-oil on panel work has a grace and graphic quality that have helped make it the best-known Renaissance work in the country.

Produced at the end of Raphael’s Florentine period, when his output still reflects a youthful interest in Leonard da Vinci, the painting apparently first made its way north of the Alps in the early 18th century during the papacy of Clement XI, landing in the Esterházy collection by 1812. Stolen in 1983, along with the museum’s prized Giorgione portrait and other works, it was recovered the following year in a Greek monastery.

Mihály Munkácsy's The Last Day of Condemned Man (1870).

Credit: Museum of Fine Arts Budapest – Hungarian National Gallery.

According to recent reports, mihály Munkácsy's The Last Day of Condemned Man (1870)Hungarian National GallerySzent György térIn Hungary’s heyday before the First World War, when Budapest began to compete with Vienna, painter Mihály Munkácsy was a national hero. Born in what is now Ukraine, then educated at the art academies of Vienna, Munich and Düsseldorf, he eventually settled in Paris, with a base of collectors stretching from Central Europe to the American Midwest. His Budapest funeral procession, in spring 1900, was witnessed by hundreds of thousands people and remains a unique event in the history of the country.

Working in a number of established genres, from history painting to portraiture, he went on to decorate both Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum and Budapest’s new Parliament building. But this breakthrough work—which scarcely gives a clue whether the condemned man in question is a criminal or a victim of injustice—remains his best known. Winning a gold medal at the 1870 Paris Salon, it was a main topic of conversation in the French capital during the final days of the doomed Second Empire.

Leonardo da Vinci's Study for the Head of a Soldier in the Battle of Anghiari (around 1504–05).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Leonardo da Vinci's Study for the Head of a Soldier in the Battle of Anghiari (around 1504–05).

Sources indicate that museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareThe MFAB's prints and drawings collection has legendary status among scholars in the field, with key works stretching from Renaissance Italy to early 20th-century Vienna, leading up to the present day. This exquisite Leonardo drawing—one of three in the collection—is a preparatory work associated with a planned mural in Florence’s Palazzo Vecchio meant to commemorate the Florentine Republic’s victory over the Duchy of Milan in 1440.

According to recent reports, left unfinished in 1506, when Leonardo himself left for Milan, the partial mural, made using an unstable oil-based technique, was nonetheless one of Cinquecento Florence’s star attractions, until its degraded version fell victim to a 1560s renovation. This red-chalk drawing of a Florentine captain, produced using a live model, is known for its depiction of intense emotion.

Hungarian crown jewels on display in the parliament building.

Photo: Schopenhauer; Courtesy Wikimedia.

In a recent development, the Holy Crown of Hungary (around 12th century)Hungarian ParliamentKossuth Lajos térThe Kingdom of Hungary—defeated in the First World War, then dismantled, degraded and now disappeared—lives on in this mysterious and glorious object. One of Europe’s oldest surviving crowns, with a lower section of enamel imagery dating all the way back to medieval Byzantium, it likely took on its present appearance in the 12th century. Containing both Latin and Greek inscriptions, and bejeweled with sapphires, garnets and amethysts, the elaborate golden crown had mystical status. It was not only a symbol, but treated as the actual incarnation of the Hungarian state, and sovereigns were not regarded as rulers until it was placed on their heads.

It has been revealed that A miraculous survivor of Hungary’s cataclysmic 20th century, it was brought back into use in 1990 following the collapse of communism. Placed on Hungary’s newly devised coat of arms, it has been on display in the national parliament since 2000.

Lili Ország’s Wall of Icons II (Blue) (1969).

Hungarian National GallerySzent György térNow regarded as one of the most important artists to emerge in Hungary after the Second World War, Ország, born into a Hungarian Jewish family in what is now Ukraine, barely escaped being deported to Auschwitz and later survived the war as a Christian convert.

Judaism, Christianity, and her own biography fuse together in her mature paintings, whose religious elements were in defiance of official communist policies. This late piece, showing a repeating Madonna-and-Child motif, is part of a series of oil-on-fiberboard works. Invoking her longstanding interest in Orthodox Christian imagery, it also alludes to her own trauma at not having had a child.

Francisco de Goya’s The Water Carrier (1808 – 12).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Francisco de Goya’s The Water Carrier (1808 – 12).

Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareGoya’s transition from a designer of Rococo tapestries to the great harbinger of Modernism is on view in this legendary painting, made during the dark years of Napoleonic Spain's Peninsular War, a guerrilla conflict that foreshadowed the atrocities of the 20th century.

An apparent genre scene showing a rustic girl carrying food and water, the painting is in fact a wartime vision of desperate heroism. The late art critic Robert Hughes was fascinated by the work, which he regarded as an “emblem of resistance.” He writes, in his 2003 biography of the artist: “You would be very grateful to see her if you were crouched stiffly behind a rock in the parching autumn sun of Aragón, breathing hot dust with the ricochets whining above.”.

Shoes on the Danube Bank memorial.

Can Togay and Gyula Pauer’s Shoes on the Danube Bank (2005)Id. Antall József rkpIn the years after the collapse of communism in 1989, the newly open societies of Central and Eastern Europe revisited the horrors of their 20th century in a number of commemorative works. This installation on the banks of the Danube, which memorialises the victims of the predominantly anti-Semitic massacres by Hungary’s fascist militias in 1944-45, is now considered one of the most artistically successful.

Comprising 60 pairs of rusty iron shoes, it was devised by Togay, a filmmaker, and executed together with Pauer, a performance artist and sculptor. Fixed in concrete but eerily scattered, the shoes—in women’s, men’s, and children’s sizes and styles—recall the militia's orders of its victims to remove their shoes before shooting them into the river.

Victor Vasarely's Zebras (1939).

© Museum of Fine Arts – Vasarely Museum, Budapest.

Victor Vasarely's Zebras (1939)Vasarely Museum BudapestSzentlélek térFor the first few decades of the 20th century, Budapest was a hothouse of the avant-garde, nurturing the likes of Modernist painter László Moholy-Nagy; Bauhaus architect Marcel Breuer; and the supreme chronicler of 1930s Paris, photographer Gyula Halász, otherwise known as Brassaï. Their work is hard to find back in Budapest, but their near contemporary, Victor Vasarely, the great pioneer of Op Art, has his own museum here.

Schooled in Modernist trends in a Budapest private art academy, Vasarely decamped for Paris in 1930, and his experiments there in the late 1930s anticipated Op Art’s illusions and manipulations by some three decades. This tempera-on-paper work was a stand-out at this year's survey of the artist, Vasarely 120, held at MFAB. It is considered a great forerunner of the movement, which Vasarely went on to promote, often in ever-larger formats, until his death in 1997, aged 90.

It has been revealed that pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Preaching of St. John the Baptist (1566).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Recent findings suggest that pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Preaching of St. John the Baptist (1566).

Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ Square.

Hungary’s longtime Habsburg rulers, residing up the Danube in Vienna, began amassing their unique collection of works by Pieter Bruegel the Elder within decades of his death in 1569. But this late work somehow got past them, ending up in the Hungarian collection of the noble Batthyány family.

A vast social panorama, with a solemnity largely missing from the artist’s more raucous works, the painting depicts nobles and soldiers, burghers and peasants, Jews and Turks, the healthy and the infirm. Nearly all are transfixed and transformed by the teachings of Christ, as spoken by St. John the Baptist, who is illuminated by little more than the attention of the crowd.

Dóra Maurer's Bent Plane with Wings (1996).

Photo © József Rosta / Ludwig Museum - MoCA, Budapest.

© SUMUS Gáyor & Maurer Foundation.

Recent findings suggest that dóra Maurer's Bent Plane with Wings (1996)Ludwig MuseumKomor Marcell utcaDuring the Orbán years, Budapest’s large national art institutions took on a retrograde atmosphere, with leading artists, like their emerging counterparts, often resorting to alternative or municipal venues. Paradoxically, it coincided with an international breakthrough of some cutting-edge figures, like Maurer, who had a 2019 survey at London’s Tate Modern.

It has been revealed that A trained graphic artist, Maurer was eventually drawn to geometric abstraction and witty illusionism. This mature acrylic-on-wood piece, acquired by the Ludwig Museum in 1998, uses lines on an apparently curved surface to create a near-sculptural, if resolutely two-dimensional piece.

This iPhone App Lets You Take Photos By Clapping

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced iPhone camera app, HyperCam Trigger, aims to make it easier for mobile photographers to nail the perfect action shot, group portrait, or lightning photo.
  • Recent findings suggest that hyperCam Trigger uses various listening and detection methods to fire the iPhone’s camera at the right moment.
  • According to recent reports, meanwhile, for group portraits, which typically rely on a self-timer, HyperCam can listen for someone in the frame to clap, triggering an immediate shot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced iPhone camera app, HyperCam Trigger, aims to make it easier for mobile photographers to nail the perfect action shot, group portrait, or lightning photo.

Recent findings suggest that hyperCam Trigger uses various listening and detection methods to fire the iPhone’s camera at the right moment. For example, when photographing sports, children, or pets, the app can trip the shutter as soon as motion appears in the frame.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, for group portraits, which typically rely on a self-timer, HyperCam can listen for someone in the frame to clap, triggering an immediate shot. Customers can customize the sensitivity for the app and the delay between detection and shooting.

In a recent development, the app’s original purpose, which remains a core focus, was to make it easier to photograph lightning. It can use sound for this as well, though thunder arrives well after the flash of lightning itself. The app can also trigger a shot when it detects a sudden surge of light hitting the camera.

It has been revealed that hyperCam can also trigger the shutter under other conditions, including camera shake, such as when the iPhone moves or tilts, or complete stability, such as when it is mounted on a tripod. Additionally, it can capture timelapse photos when it detects changes in light or motion, or wait to fire until someone in the frame smiles.

Lightning triggers are not a newly introduced concept in photography. Photographers with DSLRs and mirrorless cameras have been using them for years, and new ones hit the market every so often, like the Bolt Hunter earlier this year.

In a recent development, lightning triggers rely on the same principle as HyperCam: it is simply impossible for a photographer to manually press the shutter fast enough to catch fleeting events like lightning. Photographers can certainly try and can improve their odds by firing off long, rapid bursts of frames. However, assistance is required for consistent success.

HyperCam Trigger is available now in the App Store for free.

According to recent reports, however, some features are locked behind a paywall, including subject filters, short event video recording with frame extraction, detection zones, longer pre-trigger buffers, longer bursts, RAW recording, HDR, and more. HyperCam Pro is available for $3.99 per month, $22.99 per year, or $44.99 for lifetime access.

Industry News: Foster + Partners creates Area worktable for today's office

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Foster + Partners Industrial Design aimed to bring expressive and functional workplace design together in its modular Area table system, created with Spanish furniture brand Kettal.
  • Designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power.
  • The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Salva López.

Foster + Partners Industrial Design aimed to bring expressive and functional workplace design together in its modular Area table system, created with Spanish furniture brand Kettal.

Designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power.

The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.

Available in three diameters – 90, 160 or 450 millimetres – and either anodised or powder-coated finishes, they also bring customisable personality to the worktable.

The tabletops, meanwhile, come in shapes ranging from round to triangular and rhomboid and materials including timber, linoleum, melamine and Fenix. For larger conference or feature tables, terrazzo or marble are also options.

“Area is a collection of durable, expressive elements that define workstations and gathering points within a space to support both individual and collaborative work,” remarked Foster + Partners head of industrial design Mike Holland.

“The development of Area involved finding the right balance between structural performance, flexibility and visual simplicity,” he continued.

“The system needed to accommodate a wide variety of tabletop configurations and working arrangements, while integrating the technical infrastructure required in contemporary workplaces.”.

The Area system can be accessorised with lighting or fabric screen dividers, the infrastructure for which is built into the table. Screen dividers attach magnetically at designed points, with lighting used in combination or mounted independently.

Cables are hidden underneath the tabletop within a J-profile aluminium beam that also provides structural support, while concealed grommets provide access to plug sockets and USB-C connections.

Holland told Dezeen that designing these accessories so they could function seamlessly across a range of tabletop configurations was the key challenge of the design process for Area, alongside achieving the desired proportions and textures for the aluminium columns.

To realise their vision for the expansive system, the design team undertook extensive prototyping, including using both one-to-one and full-scale models and augmented reality (AR).

“Working with full-scale models, augmented reality and 3D printing allowed us to understand the relationship between the different components and how they would function together in real working environments,” said Holland.

“This approach was particularly important in refining the columns, assessing their proportions, and adapting the surface texture pattern at full scale. It also allowed us to evolve the design from wider diameters into more elegant and efficient forms.”.

He said that working with models and AR also allowed manufacturer Kettal to engage in the design process and contribute ideas.

“Collaboration is at the heart of our approach, and we believe it is fundamental to achieving the highest-quality results,” noted Holland.

Area was designed for the contemporary workplace, said Holland, where flexible and hybrid working have made the office primarily a place for collaboration and connection, and where the table’s modularity and adaptability allow it to evolve as needs change.

“As designers, we are interested in the points of interaction between people and buildings,” said Holland. “At the heart of industrial design lies the creation of these touchpoints through which people experience space.”.

“In the workplace, furniture plays a vital role in shaping how people engage with their environment, influencing how they occupy, navigate and connect with the spaces around them,” Holland concluded.

Part of the architecture firm Foster + Partners, Foster + Partners Industrial Design started by creating site-specific furniture, fixtures and fittings for the firm’s buildings and over the last 50 years have expanded to more stand-alone commercial products.

Some of its recent designs include the Join plywood furniture collection, Ori bird feeders and Datum porcelain tableware.

Photography by Salva López.

Apple’s Camera and Photo Software Lead Jon McCormack Has Retired

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jon McCormack, Apple’s head of photography and camera software development, has retired.
  • Bloomberg reports that McCormack retired at the end of October.
  • Industry observers note that mcCormack, who was Apple’s vice president of camera and photo engineering, has been a major figure at the Silicon Valley giant since he arrived there in 2018.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jon McCormack, Apple’s head of photography and camera software development, has retired. A spectacular photographer in his own right, McCormack is stepping away, and his departure signals a major change for Apple regardless of the circumstances.

Bloomberg reports that McCormack retired at the end of October. This information has not been independently verified, as at the time of publication, neither Apple nor McCormack has confirmed his departure.

Industry observers note that mcCormack, who was Apple’s vice president of camera and photo engineering, has been a major figure at the Silicon Valley giant since he arrived there in 2018. He oversaw the development of not only the iPhone camera system but also the camera software and all of the computational features that go along with it.

It has been revealed that he was present for every briefing and discussion about the iPhone camera system through that time and became personally known to everyone at PetaPixel. He is also regularly quoted speaking about Apple’s philosophy regarding cameras and photography.

It has been revealed that “Here’s our view of what a photograph is: The way we like to think of it is that it’s a personal celebration of something that really, actually happened,” he told PetaPixel back in 2024, just as generative AI was beginning its steady march into the creative industry. Apple has, since then, largely stayed that course.

Sources indicate that perhaps most importantly, McCormack is actually a photographer. In April, PetaPixel featured his most recent book, titled “Patterns: Art of the Natural World.”.

According to recent reports, “I grew up on a farm in the Outback, Queensland in Australia,” McCormack said. “Sheep and cattle property. We had no full-time electricity. We had a 32-volt generator that dad would run at night so that a little 12-inch black and white TV could be a thing. This is also when I got my first camera, my hand-me-down camera, and it wasn’t even my dad’s hand-me-down camera. It was my grandfather’s, a Minolta 35mm Mark IV made in either 1949 or 1950. I still have it.”.

His series made it abundantly clear that McCormack cares deeply about nature.

“My goal here is for people to look at our planet like a Fabergé egg,” McCormack explained. “It is unique, one of them in existence. It’s fragile, it’s intricate, it’s beautiful. It’s something to be protected and taken care of, and it’s something you can fall in love with.”.

It has been revealed that it’s hard to think of a greater loss for Apple than McCormack. It is unlikely that Apple will find someone who is nearly as talented or who cares as much about photography as a fine art. PetaPixel is hard-pressed to believe there was anyone better for his role at the tech giant than he was.
