  • Gruijthuijsen, a self-described “artist-driven curator,” will join the Stedelijk from EMMA – Espoo Museum of Modern Art in Finland, where he has been director since 2025, a role he holds concurrently with curator at large at Kunsthaus Zürich.
  • His vision for EMMA, a respected but relatively low-profile institution outside the Nordic region, included sustained support for artists through project funding, acquisitions and stipends, among more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has named the Dutch-born curator and art critic Krist Gruijthuijsen as its next director. He will succeed Rein Wolfs in July 2027.

Gruijthuijsen, a self-described “artist-driven curator,” will join the Stedelijk from EMMA – Espoo Museum of Modern Art in Finland, where he has been director since 2025, a role he holds concurrently with curator at large at Kunsthaus Zürich.

His vision for EMMA, a respected but relatively low-profile institution outside the Nordic region, included sustained support for artists through project funding, acquisitions and stipends, among more. Speaking to Frieze, he mentioned he envisioned opening up the floor of the Brutalist building by removing its internal walls. Related Articles Dutch Art Historian and Curator Rudi Fuchs Dies at 84 'I Live for My Art. That's Really All There Is to It': Read One of Yayoi Kusama's Final Unpublished Interviews.

Prior to EMMA, Gruijthuijsen was director of the KW Institute for Contemporary Art in Berlin, beginning in 2016. His tenure there included well-received programming, with exhibitions by artists such as Hanne Lippard, Beatriz González, and Hassan Sharif. He also curated “Martin Wong: Malicious Mischief,” which the Stedelijk co-produced and hosted from November 2023 to April 2024.

His return to Amsterdam will also mark a curatorial homecoming, as Gruijthuijsen cofounded the Kunstverein Amsterdam with Maxine Kopsa and served as its director from 2009 to 2012, a role that briefly overlapped with his time heading the MA Fine Arts department at Amsterdam’s Sandberg Instituut (2011-16).

At the Stedelijk, he will oversee the institution’s modern and contemporary art and design strategy and guide collection management and public engagement.

In a recent development, “The [Stedelijk] has long held a special place in my personal and professional life, as it does in the history of modern and contemporary art and design,” Gruijthuijsen said in a statement. “Its remarkable collection and rich legacy carry a responsibility that extends far beyond preserving the past. Above all, they call on us to engage with the present and help shape what lies ahead, with art and artists at the heart of everything we do.”.

Sources indicate that he continued, “An essential part of my role will be to deepen the museum’s relationship with Amsterdam: to make it ever more open, engaged, and connected to the city and its communities. I want the Stedelijk not only to reflect the world we live in, but also to actively contribute to shaping its future.”.

Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year revealed

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2801 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A tree-top sauna that punctures its architectural framework with the surrounding woodland has been named Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year following the announcement of all 19 architecture category winners at a party in London.
  • The 19 winners awarded at the ninth annual Dezeen Awards ceremony are located in 11 different countries, including Canada, France, India, Japan and Mexico.
  • Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna won the project of the year award in the architecture sector, it was also named leisure and wellness project of the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A tree-top sauna that punctures its architectural framework with the surrounding woodland has been named Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year following the announcement of all 19 architecture category winners at a party in London.

The 19 winners awarded at the ninth annual Dezeen Awards ceremony are located in 11 different countries, including Canada, France, India, Japan and Mexico.

Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna won the project of the year award in the architecture sector, it was also named leisure and wellness project of the year.

Leisure and wellness projects win big again.

The judges hailed the biophilic project as “beautifully minimalist with a spiritual touch of the soul”.

“It’s totally fresh, totally innovative, and never seen before,” they added.

The win marks the second consecutive year that the leisure and wellness project of the year has gone on to claim the overall sector title, following Herzog & de Meuron’s win last year.

Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi.

The winning project of the year was up against category winners including a sprawling brick-clad university building modelled on stepped wells in India, a country house with walls formed of unstabilised rammed earth in the UK and a project featuring an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through in Mexico.

A housing project that appears as if emerging from the natural landscape and a viewpoint designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the burial site of a legendary Viking were also amongst the category winners.

Read more about all the winning architecture projects below:.

Architecture project of the year and leisure and wellness project of the year: Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi.

The project is nestled within a forest in Kanagawa, southwest of Tokyo, and forms part of the Daichi Silent River retreat alongside guest cabins and additional sauna spaces.

Leisure and wellness is also about mental health, which this project addresses perfectly.

The idea for the project was to make the trees feel part of the architecture, using them as both supports and the defining feature of the pared-back structure.

“Leisure and wellness is also about mental health, which this project addresses perfectly,” said the master jury.

“It is a building that offers a spiritual connection between humans and nature.”.

House (urban) project of the year: Amami House by Sakai Architects.

Local studio Sakai Architects won urban house of the year for its off-grid home on Amami Ōshima, an island in the Amami archipelago off Japan‘s southern coast.

This house demonstrates how we can live sustainably on a small footprint, in close relationship to nature.

The design was informed by the region’s traditional materials and crafts and its development was spurred by the increase in extreme weather conditions on the island.

“This house demonstrates how we can live sustainably on a small footprint, in close relationship to nature,” the master jury noted.

“In a time of climate crisis, it offers an excellent solution for autonomy of energy, while smartly reinterpreting the arrangement and materials of a traditional Japanese house.”.

House (rural) project of the year: Jiang Deng Lu by Shisuo Design Office.

Shisuo Design Office won rural house of the year for Jiang Deng Lu in Anhui, China.

This project sits very delicately in its context and is beautiful as a result.

The compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site and made using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.

“This project sits very delicately in its context and is beautiful as a result,” noted the judges.

“Innovative in its use of available materials, the project is highly resolved, with incredible quality of light and generosity of space despite a small footprint.”.

Housing project of the year: La Querola by Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos.

Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos won housing project of the year for La Querola in Ordino, Andorra.

A deliberate provocation against the salami-type housing where repetition is at the core.

Made up of seven irregularly shaped blocks embedded into the sloping valley and clad in locally sourced slate, the building’s facades feature recessed windows and openings revealing outdoor terraces.

The judges commended the development’s trend-bucking design as a “deliberately expressionist project, celebrating forms that are not repeatable”.

Sources indicate that “It’s a deliberate provocation against the salami-type housing where repetition is at the core. It’s unconventional, unique, controversial, and a very strong statement,” they stated.

According to recent reports, recently, a fire damaged all seven buildings in the uninhabited development. The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

House renovation of the year: Haniyasu House by Aatismo.

Local architecture studio Aatismo won house renovation of the year for Haniyasu House, a home in the coastal town of Kamakura, Japan.

It is aesthetic but also functional, cleverly improving seismic stability.

The project saw the single-storey home, originally built in 1967, stripped back to its timber frame after a typhoon had left it structurally unsound, and boldly characterised with rough walls streaked with clay, soil and metal powders to evoke ceramic glazes.

The judges praised the project’s sensitivity to “the history of both the architecture and its owners”.

“It is aesthetic but also functional, cleverly improving seismic stability,” they added.

House extension of the year: Golmorad by ZAV Architects.

Iranian studio ZAV Architects won house extension of the year for its project featuring a series of overlapping arches shifts in colour from terracotta to blue in Tehran, Iran.

It’s clever and fun, with colours that reveal an intent to enjoy life.

Transforming the residence from a weekend villa into a permanent home, its arched series of overlapping arched roofs appears as if organically growing from the home.

The judges found the extension to be “playful with a sense of freedom,” adding that, “it doesn’t manipulate the old house in any way, but instead seems to organically extend it in a very unpredictable direction.”.

“It’s clever and fun, with colours that reveal an intent to enjoy life,” they mentioned.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Civic project of the year: Zando Central Market by Think Tank Architecture.

French studio Think Tank Architecture won civic project of the year for its geometric brick-and-concrete market in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo.

A bold and strong project with really interesting architectural moves.

The fresh building, with space for 20,000 vendors, replaces a historic market on the same site in the capital that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.

“A bold and strong project with really interesting architectural moves, and a capacity to serve the community in a really large-scale way,” said the master jury.

“It has a variety within it to allow a lot of activity to take place, with materials that are simple but sustainable.”.

Cultural project of the year: Ismaili Center Houston by Farshid Moussavi Architecture.

Farshid Moussavi Architects won cultural project of the year for its Ismaili Center in Houston, United States.

A very successful community space that has reinterpreted and reimagined the Ismaili-centric typology in a very contemporary rather than self-referential manner.

The building and its sprawling gardens is the first Ismaili Center in the US and is one of several around the world commissioned by the current Imam, or spiritual leader, of the Shia Ismaili Muslim community to serve as a place of worship and cultural exchange.

The judges praised it as a “very successful community space that has reinterpreted and reimagined the Ismaili-centric typology in a very contemporary rather than self-referential manner”.

“It has a stunning relationship to light, and incredible detailing and materiality,” they added.

Workplace project (small) of the year: Carpenter’s Home by Primary Architects.

Chinese studio Primary Architects won small workplace project of the year for its undulating timber roof-topped studio in Xinyang, China.

The architecture speaks of its function, offering space that cleverly facilitates different activities.

The project, a local carpenter’s studio, was designed by the practice to incorporate the craftsman’s studio, as well as a woodcraft workshop that is also open to the public.

“A beautiful project that goes above and beyond the brief,” commended the judges.

“The architecture speaks of its function, offering space that cleverly facilitates different activities.”.

Workplace project (large) of the year: Florentia Village by Turner Works.

Architecture studio Turner Works won large workplace project of the year for Florentia Village, London.

Well-thought out in terms of programme, layout and use of materials and colour.

The practice transformed an old textile manufacturing site in London’s Harringay Warehouse District into a creative hub that offers flexible workshops, studios and industrial units ranging from 46 to 1,400 square metres, alongside community spaces and a cafe.

The judges praised it as “well-thought out in terms of programme, layout and use of materials and colour,” as well as the buildings being “highly flexible, with spaces designed to reinforce a sense of community”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Education project of the year: Prestige University by Sanjay Puri Architects.

Sanjay Puri Architects won education project of the year for its sprawling brick-clad university building in Indore, India.

In a country with a tradition of beautiful campuses, but where most new constructions are based on western typologies, this one breaks the mould.

Referencing traditional stepped wells found in the country, its defining feature is its 9,000-square-metre walkable roof, which comprises 463 stepped platforms that can be used as individual social spaces or as a singular auditorium for up to 9,000 people.

“This project creates its own universe,” said the master jury.

“In a country with a tradition of beautiful campuses, but where most upcoming constructions are based on western typologies, this one breaks the mould,” they continued.

“The massing of the roof reduces scale and creates interesting courtyards, creating spaces that feel appropriate for both the place and its climate.”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Heritage project of the year: Olympics Utilities by Chartier-Corbasson Architects.

French studio Chartier-Corbasson Architectes won heritage project of the year for its transformation of a neglected underground passage beneath Paris, France.

It was a joy to see so much love put into a building typology that we might typically consider unimportant.

Located in a passage beneath the Trocadero Gardens, the studio created a public restroom, using an industrial-feeling palette of stainless and weathered steel to highlight its thoughtful, utilitarian design while giving it a new purpose.

“It was a joy to see so much love put into a building typology that we might typically consider unimportant,” stated the judges.

“The project creates architectural character, while also preserving a connection to 19th-century futuristic architecture. Unusual, but iconic.”.

Hospitality project of the year: Perma by Mold Architects.

Perma by Mold Architects in Serifos, Greece won hospitality project of the year, sponsored by Sanderson.

There is an economy of means in its relationship to the topography, which cleverly reduces the overall footprint.

Comprising five guest houses, the rugged retreat on the island of Serifos was constructed by using material extracted during construction to build much of the retreat itself, rather than removing the hillside and building on top of it.

The judges praised its “striking architecture”, noting it as “very innovative in its programmatic possibilities”.

“There is an economy of means in its relationship to the topography, which cleverly reduces the overall footprint,” they said.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Infrastructure and transport project of the year: Naples Underground Central Station by Miralles Tagliabue EMBT.

Spanish architecture studio EMBT won infrastructure and transport project of the year for Naples Underground Central Station in Italy.

A rich environment to spend time in, not just catch a train.

Contrasting its modernist surroundings with a wavy timber roof, the 10,000-square-metre building was designed to replace a previously understated metro entrance with a upcoming public plaza that felt more integrated with the surrounding city.

The judges commended the project as a “successful urban space, both elegant and spatially interesting.”.

It has been revealed that “A rich environment to spend time in, not just catch a train,” they continued. “The use of timber is also impressive.”.

Small project of the year: Ring of Bjólfur by Arkibygg Architects.

Local studios Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture won small project of the year for their mountain viewpoint in Seyðisfjörður, Iceland.

A minimal intervention that choreographs the discovery of a landscape in a simple but sophisticated way.

Designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the alleged burial site of a legendary Viking, the viewpoint improves access to a ridge on Mount Bjólfur and celebrates its varied views over the town, valley and surrounding peaks.

The master jury hailed the viewpoint as a “minimal intervention that choreographs the discovery of a landscape in a simple but sophisticated way,” adding that, “the minimal use of material maximises the experience”.

Mixed-use project of the year: York Minster Centre of Excellence by Tonkin Liu.

Architecture studio Tonkin Liu won mixed-use project of the year for its two timber buildings on either side of a Grade I-listed Gothic cathedral in York, United Kingdom.

The materiality speaks to the programming of the building, inspiring a fresh generation of makers using the space.

Named The Centre of Excellence for Heritage Craft Skills, the buildings include the rectangular Heritage Quad and the triangular Technology Hub, both of which give working stonemasons views of the historic York Minster cathedral.

“There is a real honesty in the combination of buildings, with a unique roofing structure,” remarked the judges.

“The materiality speaks to the programming of the building, inspiring a fresh generation of makers using the space,” they added.

Landscape and urban design of the year: Parque del Jaguar by Colectivo C733.

Mexican studio Colectivo C733 won landscape and urban design of the year for its work across Parque del Jaguar in Tulum, Mexico.

Despite limited budget and materials, the interventions create an intimate experience with the landscape, successfully addressing water scarcity, indigenous planting and flexibility for different community projects.

The project aims to safeguard one of the region’s crucial habitats for jaguars, whose movement through the landscape had become disrupted by roads, development and tourism.

It features an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through while protecting more than 1,000 hectares of forest, as well as a network of boundaries, access points and visitor facilities intended to protect the animals’ habitat while allowing people to explore the area.

The judges praised the project as “rooted in its context, made for locals as well as tourists,” adding that, “despite limited budget and materials, the interventions create an intimate experience with the landscape, successfully addressing water scarcity, indigenous planting and flexibility for different community projects.”.

Sustainable building of the year: Rammed Earth House by Tuckey Design Studio.

Rammed Earth house by Tuckey Design Studio in Wiltshire, United Kingdom, won sustainable building of the year, sponsored by Michelmersh.

Although large for a two-person house, it is an incredible testbed that could pave the way for more rammed earth architecture in Europe.

Built on the site of a former brickworks, the rural country house was constructed from both the clay underfoot and an aggregate made from crushed demolition waste to form unstabilised rammed earth walls.

As a form of earth construction that is largely untested at such scale in the UK, the judges commended the project as “a radical example of material innovation”.

“Although large for a two-person house, it is an incredible testbed that could pave the way for more rammed earth architecture in Europe,” they said.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Sustainable renovation of the year: De Nederlandsche Bank by Mecanoo.

Dutch firm Mecanoo won sustainable renovation of the year for its major renovation of the Netherlands’ central bank in Amsterdam.

An admirable transformation of a brutalist-era building.

The project involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault, seeing a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation’s ugliest building.

The renovation was praised as “an admirable transformation of a brutalist-era building,” by the master jury, who also noted its efforts to adapt it to a different use “while also addressing material and energy concerns.”.

  • Forot spoke about the history of the Maison Piaget, which was founded in 1874 in the idyllic village of La Côte-aux-Fées (a translation of which is “fairy hills”), as well as the company’s two manufactures, in La Côte-aux-Fées and Geneva, where the watches are conceived and produced.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that where do the worlds of art and watchmaking intersect? One place is the Andy Warhol Watch line, which the luxury Swiss watch brand Piaget has released since 2024 in collaboration with the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts.

Sources indicate that to learn more about Piaget’s history with Warhol and its ongoing partnership with the Warhol Foundation, Jean-Bernard Forot, Piaget’s Head of Patrimony, joined ARTnews for a conversation as part of the inaugural Art Week NYC, a citywide festival celebrating contemporary art. Related Articles Latest York City's Transit System Has the State's Greatest 'Underground Museum.' Here's Why It's Worth Visiting. Celebrating the Inaugural Art Week NYC, Organized by ARTnews, Art in America, and Artforum.

Forot spoke about the history of the Maison Piaget, which was founded in 1874 in the idyllic village of La Côte-aux-Fées (a translation of which is “fairy hills”), as well as the company’s two manufactures, in La Côte-aux-Fées and Geneva, where the watches are conceived and produced. Having those two locations, he stated, “creates a tension and creates a creativity that is really interesting.”.

Industry observers note that in the postwar era, Piaget became known for its bold designs featuring precious gold and ornamental stones. When it opened a US flagship on Fifth Avenue, it attracted high-profile clients like Elizabeth Taylor, Elvis Presley, and Jackie Kennedy—all of whom were subjects of Warhol’s art.

Sources indicate that warhol soon became a client of Piaget’s and befriended Yves Piaget, the firm’s longtime chairman. The Pop artist came to own at least seven Piagets, including the cushion-shaped Black Tie Watch, which Forot speculated captured Warhol’s attention for its resemblance to a TV screen. After the company reissued it decades later, collectors lovingly called it the Warhol Watch, which ultimately led Piaget to seek out a partnership with the Warhol Foundation to officially call it the “Andy Warhol Watch.”.

“We did not invent a story,” Forot said. “In fact, we are just taking a story that existed and are bringing it into the present today. That’s why there is authenticity.”.

Sources indicate that in 2025, Piaget released its “Collage” Warhol Watch, based on a Warhol self-portrait from 1986, in an edition of 50. This year’s “Camouflage” Warhol Watch, referencing the artist’s Camouflage self-portrait also from 1986, has an edition of 86 to honor the year of the work’s making. In both instances, Forot stated that Piaget has developed, over many months and several tests, a “reinterpretation” of each Warhol work, leaning into the Maison’s history of pairing gold and ornamental stones into compelling juxtapositions.

“Whether you are an artist in front of a white canvas or whether you want to create a watch or a piece of jewelry,” Forot noted, “everything starts with the same desire to create something new, to create something appealing, to try to create about beauty.”.

For more in-depth insights into Piaget’s history, philosophy of watchmaking, and collaboration with the Warhol Foundation, watch the full talk in the video above.

  • In a recent development, the latest request was first broached last summer and reiterated in the fall, when Beninese President Romuald Wadagni visited Paris and met with French President Emmanuel Macron.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A lot has happened between November 2021, when France formally returned 26 Benin Bronzes from its national collections to Benin, and today, when news of the West African nation’s latest request was reported by Le Monde. Namely, in May 2026, French Parliament passed a historic law designed to simplify the process by which artworks looted during the colonial era are returned to their nations of origin.

In a recent development, the latest request was first broached last summer and reiterated in the fall, when Beninese President Romuald Wadagni visited Paris and met with French President Emmanuel Macron. Like the 2021 repatriation, the latest request is directed to the Musée du Quai Branly – Jacques Chirac, whose collection is made up of objects from Indigenous groups in Africa, Asia, and Oceania. Related Articles Oxford University Museum Returns 39 Sets of Ancestral Remains to Naga People of India Sweden Returns Benin Bronze Trove to Nigeria, Indigenous Remains to Bolivia.

In a recent development, “We felt somewhat unsatisfied after the first return,” Alain Godonou, project manager for heritage and museums for the presidency of Benin, told Le Monde. “We drew up a second list which, in our view, meets the criteria for return under the [new] law. We are confident in our rightful claim.”.

According to recent reports, the latest request includes a divination tray and several types of weapons. But the most notable object still in the French state’s collection is a hammered iron sculpture of Gou, a god of metalworking and war. This particular representation of Gou was made by Akati Ekplekendo in the mid-19th century and was taken from Benin by the French captain Eugène Fonssagrives in 1892. The 5½-foot-tall sculpture was one of 600 objects included in the 1935 exhibition “African Negro Art” at the Museum of Modern Art in Fresh York and was also featured in the portfolio of photographs Walker Evans made in response to the show.

The latest law stipulates that a joint committee—made up, in this case, of experts from France and Benin—has two years to review new claims, at which point France’s highest administrative court will make a ruling. “In France, [the Gou] sculpture has been underestimated,” said Marie-Cécile Zinsou, a French-Beninese art historian who is a member of the committee. “Whereas in Benin it will be highly valued. It is crucial for rebuilding our memory.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that you’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover rapidly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Substantial disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

According to recent reports, going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing problems. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

In a recent development, light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

Industry observers note that working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

Recent findings suggest that an occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Sources indicate that diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

According to recent reports, the flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

In a recent development, once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that ahmed Morsi, an Egyptian-born, Upcoming York–based painter and poet who once noted he had been “displaced most of my life,” died on Wednesday at the age of 96. His death by natural causes in Cairo was confirmed his daughter Sherine Morsi.

In an Instagram post announcing the artist’s death, Sherine wrote, “His profound understanding of our shared humanity, in all its complexity, fragility, and beauty, found expression in both his art and his words.”.

Born in Alexandria, Egypt, in 1930, Ahmed Morsi studied drawing in his early years with the Italian artist Silvio Bicchi and became part of the so-called Alexandria School devoted to Surrealist imagery around the time of World War II. But, as he told ARTnews’s Alex Greenberger in 2021, “We need to distinguish between the geographic place that is Egypt’s second largest city from my ‘home.’ My Alexandria is a city of my youth and also myth and legend. This is the ‘home’ that has fueled my imagination, spilling into my poetry notebooks and pouring over my canvas. Don’t look for this Alexandria on your maps.” Related Articles Arpita Singh, Indian Painter Who Merged Fantasy and Gritty Realism, Dies at 89 Miquel Navarro, Sculptor of Large-Scale, Pared-Down Cities and Valencia's Beloved 'Pink Panther,' Dies at 81.

It has been revealed that after developing his distinctive painting style—poetic figuration with a quiet sense of fantasy suffused with muted hues—in Egypt and Iraq in the 1950s and ’60s, Morsi moved to New York in 1974 when his wife, Amany Fahmy, got a job as chief of the United Nations Arabic Translation Service. She helped translate some of Morsi’s writing, which took different forms ranging from poetry to art criticism, including the founding of Galerie 68, an influential journal devoted to Arabic modernism based in Cairo.

About his writing, which was as integral as painting to his practice, Morsi once said, “Poetry and painting may be separate media used in a constant attempt to understand the Self, but my vocabulary on paper and on canvas is one.”.

According to recent reports, in 2021, Morsi featured in MoMA PS1’s survey show “Greater Upcoming York,” and, in 2024, his work was part of Adriana Pedrosa’s “Foreigners Everywhere” exhibition for the Venice Biennale. But the world he worked in was his own: As Morsi said in a quote featured on his artist page for his gallery Salon 94, “I am not building a world—for me, that world, my world, exists and has existed since time immemorial. It is a world where everything is seen, perceived and understood differently. Your world is bound by conditioning, preconceived habits. In mine, the senses are free.”.

According to recent reports, on the morning of Frieze Abu Dhabi’s inaugural edition, Saudi Arabia’s financial center in Riyadh was reportedly attacked by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The crowd in Abu Dhabi, at least, had other things on their minds: the fair was about to open, with millions of dollars’ worth of art ready to be sold. Members of the royal family were back after getting a sneak peek yesterday, alongside politicians and celebrities including tennis star Venus Williams and architect Kulapat Yantrasast.

Industry observers note that “It’s about time. Frieze is bringing its A-game to Abu Dhabi, where they have the best museums,” Yantrasast told ARTnews, cheekily mentioning that he’s been putting dots on artworks from The Third Line, Taymour Grahne Projects, Experimenter and Pearl Lam Projects. Related Articles In the Shadow of War, Frieze Abu Dhabi Continues With 'Business as Usual' The Art Market Wanted to Go Global--It Didn't Plan for Everything That Means.

Industry observers note that the dealers were in high spirits too, as booths started to get busy an hour after the opening. At Thaddeus Ropac, three of Imran Qureshi’s Water Bodies sold for $60,000, each to a UAE-based collection, though the gallery declined to specify whether this was a private or institutional collection.

“There is a great energy around the fair in Abu Dhabi this week. We’re having good conversations with collectors who are well-informed about the artists we are presenting, and you can feel the impact of the institutional scene here,” Xenia Geroulanos, director at Thaddaeus Ropac, told ARTnews.

The fair is under the umbrella of Frieze and has rebranded from Abu Dhabi Art fair, and attendees are noticing a difference. The exhibitor list has been streamlined to 89, down from 142 last year. Dealer Asmaa Al-Shabibi told ARTnews that when she walked through the fair’s new entrance, it felt “a little bit like going into Frieze London, and it feels like a different fair.”.

Sources indicate that samy Ghiyati, co-founder of art advisory NG Partners, agreed. “The quality is definitely higher, and galleries made an effort to bring very good inventory. Usually fairs in the region are slower and sales happen over the course of several days,” he told ARTnews.

One of Ghiyati’s clients placed three orders on pieces ranging from $10,000 to $400,000. Within an hour of opening, dealer Sundaram Tagore had already placed two works on hold, one by Hiroshi Senju and another by Chun Kwang Young, ranging from $40,000 to $400,000. By late afternoon, Timothy Taylor had sold its entire solo presentation of paintings by Hilary Pecis to institutional and private collections in the region and internationally, to the price of $65,000-$205,000. The London-based antiquities gallery David Aaron sold a 2,000-year-old funerary stele for a seven-figure sum to a private collector, while Dubai-based Taymour Grahne Projects also sold out its booth of mosaic works depicting 70s-era architecture in Abu Dhabi.

It has been revealed that regional collectors reportedly spent big at Frieze Abu Dhabi. Iris Projects sold two works by Shamsa Al Omaira, a sculpture acquired by a latest foundation in the UAE for $32,000 and an acrylic on canvas by Juma Al Haj for $20,400. UAE-based collectors also bought two ceramics by Eman Al Hashemi, priced at $17,000 and $15,000, an oil pastel on linen by Dhabia Al Qubaisi for $10,500, and a photograph by Ammar Al Attar for $12,500.

Sources indicate that by then, Lawrie Shabibi had sold seven pieces by artists Hamra Abbas and Shaikha Al Mazrou, priced from $10,000 to $120,000. “People are recognizing the work when they’re coming here,” said the gallery’s cofounder Asmaa Al-Shabibi, referring to a latest client who bought a work by Al Mazrou, who has a solo exhibition at the Cultural Foundation.

Rayan Ben El Mlih, sales and marketing manager at Waddington Custot, told ARTnews that a large contingent of collectors with reserves hailed from Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Qatar and Bahrain. The gallery brought works by Etel Adnan, Sophia Vari and Fabienne Verdier.

Dealers noted that local collectors, some of whom began their collections by acquiring Western artists, are now deepening their collections with more historical pieces by regional artists.

In a recent development, “We’ve been seeing European collectors diversifying their collections, too,” said Ghiyati. Dubai’s Carbon 12 sold a painting and a sculpture by 28-year-old artist Sarah Al Mehairi, as well as two works by Mexican artist Edgar Orlaineta, priced between $17,570 and $35,000 (€16,000-€32,000).

“We’ve engaged mostly with collectors that we’ve cultivated relationships with for a while, and this is our home fair,” Judy Karkour, associate director of Carbon 12, told ARTnews.

In a recent development, collectors are branching out beyond SWANA this year, with notable interest in art from the African continent and its diaspora and Latin America. Meanwhile this year’s Frieze Masters section is dedicated to trade across the Indian Ocean, taking its cues from the Louvre Abu Dhabi’s current exhibition “Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean.” An hour into the fair, Efie Gallery had placed two works by Malian artist Abdoulaye Konaté on reserve, both priced between $45,000 to $65,000, in addition to two works by Cuban artist Maria Magdalena Campos Pons ($27,500-$55,000).

“Frieze Abu Dhabi has got off to a strong start for us with a high volume of enquiries in the first few hours from both institutions and private collections,” Kwame Mintah, cofounder of Efie Gallery, told ARTnews, which specializing in artists of African descent. “One of the more encouraging developments across the Gulf has been the gradual maturation of its collecting community, accompanied by a growing appreciation for artistic practices beyond established geographical and institutional frameworks,” he added.

Sources indicate that at Daniel Crouch Rare Books, a private collector bought the first map to name Abu Dhabi, dated to 1832. While dealer Daniel Crouch declined to say how much the map sold for, he priced the booth’s total value between $10,073 and $1.19 million (AED 37,000 to AED 4.4 million).

Recent findings suggest that “Abu Dhabi is becoming a cultural hub in the region with a lot of development,” Crouch stated. “It’s the logical place to come to for dealing in the larger Indian Ocean region and the Louvre Abu Dhabi exhibition has attracted quite a lot of attention—we’ve obviously jumped into it with alacrity.” London-based antiquities gallery ArtAncient, carrying pieces ranging from $5,000 to $5 million, sold a collection of shipwreck jewels for an undisclosed sum—the gallery also had a visit from Venus Williams, who was admiring the Graeco-Roman mummy portrait Portrait L, which had recently been dubbed the “Mona Lisa of the Middle East.”.

Sources indicate that throughout the opening, the blue-chip-leaning powerhouses, including Gagosian, Pace Gallery, Thaddaeus Ropac, and Victoria Miro, boasted crowded booths. Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

📅 09 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that ah, creatine!
  • Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells.
  • Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Recent findings suggest that now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a big-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s key to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

According to recent reports, the same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

It has been revealed that beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

According to recent reports, thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health issues that go beyond your hairstyle.

Furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

Working between Japan and Europe, Kuma and Elsa are creating an architectural vocabulary that feels both regionally distinctive and deeply connected to its surroundings.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Landing, a beloved Los Angeles gallery whose program was defined by its unique pairings of historical and contemporary artists, revealed that it had closed. Its last exhibition was a one-night only solo for Maxwell Hendler staged on October 29.

On the gallery’s website, founder and owner Gerard O’Brien wrote, “the Landing Gallery at 5118 W Jefferson Blvd is now closed. We are no longer programming at this location. We are deeply grateful to the artists, collectors, collaborators, and community who have been fellow participants in our engagements. It has been a privilege to champion extraordinary artists, present ambitious exhibitions, and create a space for meaningful exchange and discovery.” Related Articles Two More Vienna Galleries Close, Citing 'No New Collectors' and 'Challenging' Financial Landscape Prairie, Chicago Gallery That Put Conceptualism Ahead of Commercialism, Closes After Nearly a Decade.

In an Instagram post, Gerard O’Brien put it more simply, “End of an era … 22 years of Gallery spaces in Los Angeles, Reform Galley 2004-2019 … the Landing Gallery 2012 -2026 … onwards. thank you Los Angeles❣️”.

O’Brien founded the Landing in 2012 as an off-shoot of his design-focused Reform Gallery. “I never really thought there was a massive difference,” he said of the distinction between art and design. He chose the name for its original location, a spot within Reform: “he cleared out the landing atop a short staircase in his furniture gallery and dedicated it to demonstrates of art, bringing in work by artists both contemporary and historical to display just above his design wares,” as a 2016 blog post by book publisher Phaidon reported.

In 2015, O’Brien decided that it was time for the Landing to grow, opening in a 2,800-square-foot gallery space on Jefferson Boulevard with a solo show for the late California artist JB Blunk.

It has been revealed that over the years, the Landing would become known for its pairings of historical and contemporary artists. At the time of its closing, its roster included four deceased artists (Jeremy Anderson, Richard Bowman, Leslie Kerr, and Fred Reichman) and five living contemporary artists (Yevgeniya Baras, Ryan Fenchel, Matt Phillips, Jonathan Ryan, and Amanda Valdez).

The gallery was also known for regularly staging off-kilter group exhibitions, with titles like “Rat Bastard Protective Association” (2016), “The Useful and the Decorative” (2017), “Newly introduced Iconography: Artists Raising Children” (2021), and “Consensual Ennui (2023). The first of these, “3 Women” (2016) took its name from a 1977 Robert Altman film as a way “to create a cross-generational dialogue that explores the intersections of craft and fine art, influence and homage,” per a release. It featured the work of Lenore Tawney from the 1960s and ’70s paired with textile pieces by Tanya Aguiñiga and paintings by Loie Hollowell. The exhibition marked the first time Tawney’s work had been exhibited in LA in nearly 50 years.

In an Artforum review, Erin Kimmel wrote, “The Landing’s handsome, restrained exhibition showcased the exquisite detail of [Tawney’s] works, which reward prolonged scrutiny with seemingly boundless formal revelations.”.

To mark its 10th anniversary at its Jefferson Boulevard space, the Landing mounted a two-part anniversary exhibition. The first part, which opened in November 2025, focused on contemporary art and design and featured the work of Ruth Asawa, Wallace Berman, Bruce Conner, Lyne Foulkes, and Doyle Lane. The second part, which opened this past April, featured gallery artists as well as others who had exhibited there, including Brenda Goodman, Sam Jablon, and Lukas Geronimas.

Recent findings suggest that in a release for part one, O’Brien wrote, “10 Year brings together the feeling of the earliest days of the Landing Gallery when two years of exhibitions took place inside Reform Gallery on Melrose Avenue. Exhibiting art in a salon style in dialogue with decorative arts is how tL began.”.

It has been revealed that the Landing’s closure is the latest in an extended wave of closures that began in mid-2025. Los Angeles galleries have particularly been affected, with Murmurs, the Box, LA Louver, and Blum all shuttering, along with the LA outposts of Marian Goodman Gallery and Tanya Bonakdar.

Industry observers note that in his statement on the gallery’s website, O’Brien added, “While our gallery doors have closed, our commitment to art and artists continues. Watch this space for news of future offsite exhibitions, activations, and special projects. Thank you for being part of the Landing’s ongoing narrative.”.

It has been revealed that imagine stepping off a long-haul flight, exhausted and slightly rumpled, and walking into the Park Hyatt Tokyo — the hotel made iconic by *Lost in Translation* — and being handed a room key to a suite with floor-to-ceiling views of Mount Fuji. Or picture arriving at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme, where Haussmann architecture frames your every view and the concierge greets you by name. Or standing in the Park Hyatt Fresh York, 25 floors above Midtown, watching the city sprawl in every direction from a room that costs more per night than most people's monthly car payment. Now imagine paying nearly nothing for it. That's the power of the World of Hyatt award chart — and the Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community's collective jaw drop: a single night at the Park Hyatt New York regularly retails for **$1,200–$2,000**. The Park Hyatt Tokyo commands **$800–$1,500** per night. The Park Hyatt Paris? Easily **$1,000+** in peak seasons. Yet every one of these properties sits at **Category 7**, bookable for just **25,000–30,000 World of Hyatt points** per night. At 30,000 points for a $1,500 room, you're extracting **5 cents per point (cpp)** — in a world where most loyalty programs are engineered to deliver 1–1.5 cpp if you're lucky. The CPP range for this sweet spot runs from **2.7 cpp all the way to 6.7 cpp**, meaning even a modest redemption delivers 2–3x the value of a typical points transaction. Why does this gap exist? Because Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** anchored to categories, not real-time cash pricing. When demand spikes — New Year's Eve in New York, cherry blossom season in Tokyo, Paris Fashion Week — cash rates explode upward while your points cost stays locked. The hotel's revenue management team can't touch your award rate. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community is built to exploit. This isn't aspirational travel for the ultra-wealthy. This is FI-minded travel: understanding the system, earning points intentionally, and converting them into experiences that would otherwise require an extra year of saving. A two-night stay at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for 60,000 points — points you can earn from a single credit card welcome bonus — is the kind of redemption that reframes what financial independence actually looks like in practice.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt prices its awards on a fixed category chart, while Park Hyatt properties punch dramatically above their category ceiling in cash value.

Here's how the Hyatt award chart works: properties are assigned to Categories 1 through 8, with standard award nights running from 3,500 points (Cat 1) up to 45,000 points (Cat 8). Park Hyatt properties — the absolute pinnacle of the Hyatt portfolio, a collection of ultra-luxury city hotels that competes directly with Four Seasons and Ritz-Carlton — fall predominantly into Category 7 (25,000 points/night) and Category 8 (40,000 points/night). But unlike Four Seasons or Ritz-Carlton, which have largely abandoned fixed award charts in favor of dynamic pricing that tracks cash rates, Hyatt has held the line on fixed pricing. This is a rare and increasingly endangered feature in hotel loyalty, which is exactly why the ChooseFI community should be actively using it now.

According to recent reports, the transfer path that makes this accessible is Chase Ultimate Rewards. Chase transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant — meaning you can spot availability, transfer your points, and book within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, also instantly, giving you two powerful earning pipelines into the same program.

Sources indicate that this matters enormously for strategy. Chase Ultimate Rewards is arguably the most flexible points currency in travel rewards — earned through cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve — and the fact that it flows directly into Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio without any degradation is a genuine gift. 30,000 Chase UR points become exactly 30,000 Hyatt points. No conversion fees, no waiting period, no surprises.

Another critical mechanism: World of Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award redemptions. With hotel awards this is less of an issue than with airline programs, but it reflects Hyatt's broader philosophy of clean, predictable award pricing. What you see is what you pay — taxes and fees on hotel awards are typically minimal.

Now layer in Globalist status, and the value compounds further. World of Hyatt's top-tier elite status (earned at 60 qualifying nights per year) unlocks complimentary suite upgrades at check-in (space available) and free breakfast for two guests daily. If you're a Globalist checking into the Park Hyatt Latest York and you receive a suite upgrade, you've just added hundreds of dollars of daily value to an already exceptional redemption — and free breakfast at a Park Hyatt can easily run $60–$90 per person.

In a recent development, the booking window is 395 days out, which matters for high-demand dates. Understanding that you can search and book nearly 13 months in advance is your single biggest tactical advantage for locking in prime dates.

In a recent development, finally, it's worth understanding what you're getting at the property level. Park Hyatt is not Hyatt Regency or even Andaz — it's Hyatt's true ultra-luxury tier, with butler service, marble bathrooms, curated art collections, and some of the best city-view room designs in the world. The points-to-experience ratio here is genuinely exceptional.

  • Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

Recent findings suggest that wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:.

Recent findings suggest that caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Recent findings suggest that chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner looks suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future plans feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

If imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love intends a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

Sources indicate that shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

Recent findings suggest that no respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

If they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

Sources indicate that if your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

Industry observers note that true love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

It has been revealed that still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Industry observers note that are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.

Tech Report: Isern Serra designs bold colour-blocked interiors for Barcelona pilates studio

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spanish design practice Isern Serra combined organic architectural forms with a vibrant colour palette for Circl, a fitness studio and matcha cafe located in Barcelona’s historic Eixample district.
  • Set just below street level, the 180-square-metre space was designed to offer an escape from the busy city centre and contains an entrance cafe, reception area, changing rooms, bathrooms and a pilates studio.
  • “The project began with the idea of bringing together two worlds: pilates and matcha,” Isern Serra told Dezeen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Salva López.

Spanish design practice Isern Serra combined organic architectural forms with a vibrant colour palette for Circl, a fitness studio and matcha cafe located in Barcelona’s historic Eixample district.

Set just below street level, the 180-square-metre space was designed to offer an escape from the busy city centre and contains an entrance cafe, reception area, changing rooms, bathrooms and a pilates studio.

“The project began with the idea of bringing together two worlds: pilates and matcha,” Isern Serra told Dezeen.

“Although different in nature, both share a common philosophy centred on wellbeing, balance and the connection between body and mind,” he continued.

“Architecture plays an essential role in this experience, accompanying visitors on a gradual transition from the energy of the city towards a more intimate and introspective environment.”.

His studio introduced a series of colour-blocked spaces to guide customers through different phases of the interior, with colours that were specifically chosen to correspond to the function and tone of each area.

“This vision of wellbeing takes shape through a carefully choreographed sequence of spaces, where each change in level, colour and atmosphere guides people away from the bustle of the city and towards an increasingly introspective environment,” stated Serra.

In a recent development, serra combined cream banquette seating with dark wooden tables and alabaster sconces to create a calm, meditative environment for the cafe part of the space. A sculptural, mirrored service counter was also incorporated to reflect natural light around the space.

To signal the transition into the pilates studio, the designers introduced a deep-green reception hallway with tiered seating blocks and a spherical light installation.

The bright green circulation area is connected by an open archway and features curved architectural volumes that house the changing rooms, bathrooms and a water fountain.

Another rounded archway then leads to the main studio.

The main pilates studio was designed as a white space to reflect the coloured light from a sculptural LED light installation attached to the vaulted ceiling.

The aim was to create diverse exercise environments and enable the lighting to control the mood and energy of the space.

“The white surfaces act as a neutral canvas for coloured light, allowing different hues to transform the atmosphere,” Serra noted.

“This system also offers flexibility for brand collaborations, as the lighting can be adapted to reflect different identities and experiences,” he added.

In the studio, the designers used mirrored walls to create the illusion of a circular room and added full-length perimeter curtains to soften the space’s texture.

Other interior projects recently featured on Dezeen include Matteo Thun designs for Milan’s Torre Velasca skyscraper and SABO’s design of an apartment on Manhattan’s Lower East Side.

Photography by Salva López.

Say What? 7 Tips to Unclog Your Blocked Ears

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears.
  • Sources indicate that whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort.
  • Industry observers note that clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears. There are many easy ways to get relief at home. Whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort. Thankfully, there are several effective methods to help unclog your ears and restore your hearing. Listen up! Why are my ears clogged? Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum. Here are the most common ways your ears can get blocked: Earwax in the outer ear helps prevent particles and excess water from entering the middle ear. However, if earwax builds up too much outside the eardrum, it can cause a blockage. If you’ve been swimming recently, some water might be stuck in your ear canal, pushing against your eardrum. When that water hangs around too long, it can lead to a swimmer’s ear, an outer ear infection. Sinus infections, ear infections, and Eustachian tube dysfunction can pressure your eardrum’s inner side. Allergies can cause uncomfortable inflammation and congestion in your ears. Your sinuses, throat, and ears are connected, so when you feel stuffed up and sniffly, your inner ear feels the pain too. Changes in air pressure, like when you fly, can cause uncomfortable ear pressure. Best clogged ear remedies 1. Pop and unclog The easiest way to unclog your ears is by “popping” them. Just pinch your nose shut, seal your lips, and gently blow. This simple technique, known as the Valsalva maneuver, won’t clear earwax or fluid but is a common trick people use on planes. 2. Swallow, yawn, or chew The Eustachian tubes connect your middle ear to the back of your throat. They briefly open when you swallow, yawn, or chew. Altitude changes can cause these tubes to close, but chewing gum or yawning can help reopen them. Alternatively, you can try the Toynbee maneuver, where you hold your nose and swallow. 3. Ear drops Over-the-counter (OTC) ear drops can soften and dissolve excess earwax. If you prefer a DIY approach, warm a small amount of mineral oil and use an eye dropper to apply a few drops into your ear for a few minutes. Pro tip: Baby oil or olive oil can also be used, but make sure it’s not too hot. Additionally, diluted hydrogen peroxide drops can be helpful. 4. Warmth and gravity To loosen up clogged earwax, use a warm, damp washcloth as a compress. Lie down with the clogged ear facing down against the heated washcloth. Gravity and heat will help the earwax move along more easily. 5. Hit the steam room Steam can help drain sinuses and alleviate pressure in your inner ear. Close the bathroom door, let the hot shower run for a while, and then luxuriate with deep, cleansing breaths. 6. Take allergy medication Because your throat, sinuses, and ears are interconnected, any sickness affecting your sinuses or throat can also impact your ears. Over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal sprays can relieve sniffles, coughs, and ear discomfort. 7. Rinse away the gunk Rinsing your nasal passages with a medication-free saline solution can help reduce congestion and clear out mucus that might be causing ear blockage. You can also consider investing in a nasal irrigation system for more thorough mucus clearing. When to see your doctor Have you been unable to unclog your ears for a few days, or are you experiencing severe pain, fever, dizziness, hearing loss, fluid discharge, or unusual odor? If so, it’s crucial to contact your healthcare provider promptly. These symptoms may indicate an infection that needs medical attention. What not to do when you have clogged ears Cotton swabs: Q-tips and other cotton swabs to remove earwax can push it further into your ear canal, so don’t do it. Candling: Ear candles might seem like a fun party trick, but there’s no science to prove they work, and they’ve been shown to cause injuries. Sprays: Decongestant nasal sprays can be helpful, but using them too long can lead to rebound congestion. Drying solutions: A few drops of rubbing alcohol or a mixture of one part vinegar and one part alcohol can help dry out the ears when you have a swimmer’s ear. However, doing this regularly can lead to irritation. Takeaway Clogged ears are often caused by earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure. You can use over-the-counter or DIY ear drops, irrigation kits, or warm compresses to unblock your ears. Antihistamines or nasal sprays can also help relieve clogs caused by allergies. PSA: Consult a healthcare provider if your blocked ears are painful or at-home remedies don’t work.

To loosen up clogged earwax, use a warm, damp washcloth as a compress. Lie down with the clogged ear facing down against the heated washcloth. Gravity and heat will help the earwax move along more easily.

Steam can help drain sinuses and alleviate pressure in your inner ear. Close the bathroom door, let the hot shower run for a while, and then luxuriate with deep, cleansing breaths.

Because your throat, sinuses, and ears are interconnected, any sickness affecting your sinuses or throat can also impact your ears.

Over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal sprays can relieve sniffles, coughs, and ear discomfort.

According to recent reports, rinsing your nasal passages with a medication-free saline solution can help reduce congestion and clear out mucus that might be causing ear blockage. You can also consider investing in a nasal irrigation system for more thorough mucus clearing.

Have you been unable to unclog your ears for a few days, or are you experiencing severe pain, fever, dizziness, hearing loss, fluid discharge, or unusual odor? If so, it’s crucial to contact your healthcare provider promptly. These symptoms may indicate an infection that needs medical attention.

Clogged ears are often caused by earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure. You can use over-the-counter or DIY ear drops, irrigation kits, or warm compresses to unblock your ears. Antihistamines or nasal sprays can also help relieve clogs caused by allergies.

PSA: Consult a healthcare provider if your blocked ears are painful or at-home remedies don’t work.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI is almost here, and it reminds us that a good open world needs more than a lot of buildings. It needs places that feel as though they existed before you arrived and will carry on after you've driven off. In GTA 6, Rockstar is trying to achieve that by thinking about the people behind every home, business and building in Leonida.

According to recent reports, “For every visual design, we are getting into the heads of the people who would have inhabited that place and role-playing how the final look would have come about,” says Miriam Bellard, Vice President of Art: Visual Development. “Would they have hired an architect or DIY’d it? Are they trying to express their status and prestige, or is it all about comfort and practicalities? Are they messy or tidy? What is their taste?”.

Recent findings suggest that it's a wonderfully practical way to approach world-building, and after playing GTA 6 for three weeks, I can say each building feels unique yet makes sense, both to explore and to use within the game's world. Rather than designing a building as an isolated piece of architecture, the team imagines the decisions behind it. That gives each place a personality, whether it's somewhere industrial, scruffy, decadent or dangerous.

It has been revealed that “I love that we get to do that for such a wide variety of people and places,” Bellard adds. “Everything from industrial to scruffy to decadent to dangerous. We get to design all of that – and it’s lots of fun!”.

Sources indicate that that variety matters in a world inspired by Florida, where the landscape shifts between sun-soaked beaches, retirement communities, rural enclaves, and high-end shopping districts. John Macpherson, Senior Design Director: World & Population, notes reference trips and time spent with locals helped the team capture the state's “raw energy and vibrant chaos”.

The result is a world where even a building's appearance can tell you something about who lives or works there, and I found it can also help you initiative heists and robberies by understanding the flow of a bank or store. Moreover, Rockstar's designers and artists have played with Vice City and the State's history, building wear and tear and architectural trends into its world. In GTA 6, architecture is another way to get to know Leonida.

It has been revealed that ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian debuted Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that tangerines are not just tasty — they’re a powerhouse of nutrients. Packed with tangy flavor and vibrant orange color, these citrus delights offer a host of health benefits. From boosting your immune system to rejuvenating your skin, tangerines are nutrient-rich allies for your well-being. Let’s delve into their nutritional profile and discover why they’re a smart addition to your diet.

Tangerines are nutritional powerhouses. Here’s what each of these little champs pack under their orange belts:.

Industry observers note that tangerines are teeny cousins of the orange but with a thinner, easier-to-peel skin. They boast a sweet and juicy flavor and pack a ton of vitamins, particularly vitamin C, as well as minerals like potassium, antioxidants, and dietary fiber.

In a recent development, these tiny bursts of sunshine have many benefits that can significantly enhance your health. Here’s why you might want to make tangerines a regular part of your diet:.

In a recent development, tangerines are loaded with vitamin C, turning them into tiny, tasty guardians for your health. This crucial vitamin supercharges your immune system by enhancing the function and effectiveness of white blood cells, which are essential for fighting off pathogens and infections. By improving the activity and response of these cells, vitamin C helps your body combat a wide range of infections more effectively.

Therefore, regular consumption of these mini-oranges satisfies your taste buds and boosts your body’s defense mechanisms — a win-win!

Industry observers note that want that glow? Tangerines have got you covered. They’re high in potassium, a real game-changer for regulating hydration and balancing fluid levels in your skin cells. This essential mineral keeps your skin cells plump and hydrated, warding off pesky, dry, dull patches.

Plus, potassium supports the removal of toxins and wastes, which means clearer, more radiant skin.

Tangerines are also a fantastic source of vitamin A, which strengthens the outer layer of your skin, smoothing out wrinkles and reducing fine lines. Along with vitamin C, it’s a potent antioxidant, protecting your skin from the damaging and aging effects of free radicals.

Are you having tummy troubles? Tangerines can help with a fiber boost that keeps things moving smoothly along your digestive tract.

In a recent development, these zesty little superheroes are your gut’s new best friends. They’re loaded with fiber that bulks up and softens things down there, making your bathroom visits smooth and speedy. This fruity fix helps manage everything from irregular pit stops to those bloated bleurgh days.

Fiber also balances your gut flora, promoting a healthy microbial environment in your intestines. This balance is crucial for optimal digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune function.

So, grab a tangerine to remedy your belly blues next time your gut feels out of whack.

Recent findings suggest that tangerines are a dynamo when it comes to battling serious health baddies like cancer and heart disease. These little orange wonders are loaded with flavonoids, natural compounds that help with heart health and cancer prevention.

In a recent development, flavonoids help relax the blood vessels, lowering blood pressure levels and reducing the strain on your heart. This helps keep your ticker ticking smoothly and reduces the risk of cardiovascular diseases like heart attacks and strokes.

According to recent reports, but wait, there’s more! When it comes to cancer, flavonoids mess with the bad guys — cancer cells — stopping them from multiplying and spreading their nonsense around your body.

In a recent development, keep your peepers sharp with a dose of vitamin A from tangerines. This essential nutrient and compounds like beta-carotene shield your eyes from age-related concerns and support healthy vision. It plays a key role in creating rhodopsin, a protein in your eyes that allows you to see in low-light conditions.

Munching on tangerines helps keep your night vision in superhero shape and supports overall eye function, keeping your peepers sharp and responsive.

Furthermore, tangerines contain other essential eye health nutrients, like lutein and zeaxanthin. These antioxidants are found in high concentrations in the retina, where they help filter blue light and prevent oxidative damage, further protecting the eyes from conditions like cataracts.

Sure, tangerines are delish and make your taste buds do a happy dance, but they’re also packed with nutrients that can seriously amp up your well-being.

It has been revealed that from giving your immune system a high-five to keeping your heart beating like a healthy drum, tangerines are basically wellness wrapped in a bright orange peel. So, go grab one and make it your main squeeze!

Cricut Maker 5 review: A smaller, smarter cutting machine for serious crafters
